turns.en: Sherif, thank you so much for being here. Welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Sherif，非常感谢你来到节目。欢迎来到播客。

turns.en: It's so awesome to be here. Thank you for having me. Long time listener, first time caller, so it feels surreal, but good to be here.
turns.zh: 很高兴能来。谢谢邀请。我是长期听众，第一次来电，感觉有点超现实，但很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: I get that a lot. You are head of AI and product craft at Atlassian. You and your team build some of the most important and influential products in the field of product. Jira, ever heard of it? Something that is very cool about you and your job is you spend a lot of time thinking about what makes a great product manager, how to develop great product managers, how to hire product managers. You spend a lot of time on the craft and the skill of being a product manager. Let me ask just this big question and see where it goes. What makes a great product manager?
turns.zh: 我经常听到这种话。你是 Atlassian 的 AI 与产品工艺负责人。你和你的团队打造了产品领域一些最重要、最有影响力的产品。Jira，听说过吗？关于你和你的工作，很酷的一点是，你花很多时间思考什么造就了伟大的产品经理、如何培养伟大的产品经理、如何招聘产品经理。你花很多时间在产品经理的工艺和技能上。让我问这个大的问题，看看会聊到哪里。什么造就了伟大的产品经理？

turns.en: In any medium to large organization, I'm going to focus on that because I think it's quite different from a startup. I think that the largest, most important part of their job, to use a phrase that everyone loves using today, context, is I think they're literally filling context. They're filling context with humans and I guess these days with agents too. But they're the ones who realize that the best way I can advance this product is not by me taking all the decisions and all that stuff. It's one of my popular misconceptions I love to debunk: product managers don't own all the decisions. But it's about if they can build a shared brain with their team, their cross-functional team, especially their engineers. I always say three types of context to my teams: you have the customer context, you have the product and market context, and you have the business that you operate in context. And you're always filling context gaps. Like the hardest thing I've had to do, Lenny, ever—someone asked me the other day, what's the hardest thing you've ever done at Atlassian? And I feel like without a doubt it's just scaling product teams. Everything breaks. Trust breaks, shared brains break, us and them culture starts forming. In any scaled organization more than 20, 30 people you're going to run into this. So having a job of building a shared brain as a group on those three contexts becomes key because if you can empower everyone with that context, they can move faster. I always say to PMs, your job is to stay away from the Jira backlog. And they're like, wait, what? You work at Atlassian, you can't say that. And I'm like, no, no, hang on a second, hear me out for a sec. Run away from your backlog because why is it that you think some card is more important than another card? There's some context that you have that the rest of your team doesn't. So how can you empower your product engineers, your feature leads, your designers, etc. with that context so that they can make those decisions themselves? Now granted you may never work yourself out of a job, but you're always filling context gaps. Because it might be a vision gap this year, next quarter might be a customer gap, might be a landscape gap. Like, you're always trying to fill context. Now I think the best PMs are the ones that are thinking about building a shared brain at any scale product or software team.
turns.zh: 在任何中大型组织中——我会聚焦于此，因为我认为这与初创公司相当不同——我认为他们工作中最大、最重要的部分，用一个今天大家都爱用的词来说，就是上下文。我认为他们实际上是在填充上下文。他们在为人填充上下文，我想如今也在为智能体填充上下文。但他们是那些意识到推进这个产品的最好方式不是我做出所有决定等等的人。这是我喜欢打破的一个流行误解：产品经理并不拥有所有决定权。关键在于他们能否与团队、跨职能团队，尤其是工程师，建立一个共享大脑。我总是对我的团队说三种上下文：你有客户上下文，你有产品和市场上下文，还有你运营所在的业务上下文。你总是在填补上下文缺口。比如我做过的最难的事情，Lenny，曾经有人问我，你在 Atlassian 做过的最难的事情是什么？我觉得毫无疑问就是扩展产品团队。一切都会崩溃。信任崩溃，共享大脑崩溃，我们与他们文化开始形成。在任何超过二三十人的规模化组织中，你都会遇到这个问题。所以，作为一个团队，在这三种上下文上建立共享大脑的工作就变得至关重要，因为如果你能用这些上下文赋能每个人，他们就能更快行动。我总是对产品经理说，你的工作就是远离 Jira 待办列表。他们会说，等等，什么？你在 Atlassian 工作，你不能这么说。我说，不，不，等一下，听我说完。远离你的待办列表，因为为什么你认为某张卡片比另一张更重要？你拥有一些团队其他人没有的上下文。那么你如何用这些上下文赋能你的产品工程师、功能负责人、设计师等，让他们自己做出这些决定？当然，你可能永远不会让自己失业，但你总是在填补上下文缺口。因为今年可能是愿景缺口，下个季度可能是客户缺口，可能是格局缺口。你总是在试图填补上下文。现在我认为最好的产品经理是那些思考在任何规模的产品或软件团队中建立共享大脑的人。

turns.en: So a big implication of this advice—because I don't think many people would think this is what makes a great PM. This is a really interesting and unique take, this idea of just providing context for the team versus—you even said this—like your job as a PM is not to make the decisions, it's to help your team make better decisions and through that it's give them context. So kind of the implication here is your job is to help the team have all of the information such that they can all make the right decision versus you having to convince them or be the decision maker.
turns.zh: 所以这个建议的一个重大含义——因为我认为很多人不会认为这是造就伟大产品经理的因素。这是一个非常有趣和独特的观点，即只为团队提供上下文，而不是——你甚至说过——作为产品经理，你的工作不是做决定，而是帮助团队做出更好的决定，并通过这种方式给他们上下文。所以这里的含义是，你的工作是帮助团队拥有所有信息，以便他们都能做出正确的决定，而不是你必须说服他们或成为决策者。

turns.en: Yeah, I remember early on my career—I remember sitting down with my manager saying like this is insane. I have so many decisions I need to make. The team's blocked on me. I need to move in this direction and that direction, that direction. And she looks at me after me venting for like 10 minutes, staring in the eye, and I could tell she was sort of looking past me, not really listening. And she says, Sherif, you just need to spend more time on the strategic things. And I'm like, how do you have time for these things? Like I'm too busy planning the sprint, working on what we're doing next, etc. And you realize that the best way to make you and the team scale is by making sure that everyone has a shared brain. You know, simple as it can go by simple examples like I try never to do customer interviews without engineers in the room. Like you're building context in your brain. Sure, I can do the interview then get an agent to summarize all that stuff and hand it off to a human and say, look, here's the findings. But if you're sitting in the same call as me, Lenny, your aha moments and the empathy that you build for the customer is 100 times better than someone who's just handing over reports of here's my customer findings. So that's an example of filling customer context.
turns.zh: 是的，我记得在我职业生涯早期，我和我的经理坐在一起说，这太疯狂了。我有这么多决定要做。团队被我阻塞了。我需要朝这个方向、那个方向、那个方向推进。她在我发泄了大约 10 分钟后看着我，盯着我的眼睛，我能看出她有点越过我在看，并没有真正在听。她说，Sherif，你只需要花更多时间在战略性的事情上。我说，你怎么有时间做这些事？我太忙了，比如规划冲刺、处理我们下一步要做什么等等。然后你意识到，让你和团队扩展的最好方式是确保每个人都有一个共享大脑。你知道，简单来说，就像我尽量从不在没有工程师在场的情况下做客户访谈。就像你在你的大脑中构建上下文。当然，我可以做访谈，然后让一个智能体总结所有内容，交给一个人说，看，这是发现。但如果你和我坐在同一个通话中，Lenny，你的顿悟时刻和你对客户建立的同理心比那些只是递交客户发现报告的人要好 100 倍。所以这是填充客户上下文的一个例子。

turns.en: How can I do that in a way that more engineers feel empowered for that? But you know, product and strategy context—you might get your team involved in visioning together, looking at the market landscape together, and trying out different tools together, rather than one person doing it and coming down from the mountain handing over these instructions.
turns.zh: 我怎样才能让更多工程师在这方面感到被赋能？但你知道，在产品与战略背景下——你可以让团队一起参与愿景规划，一起观察市场格局，一起尝试不同的工具，而不是一个人做完后像从山上下来一样把指令丢给大家。

turns.en: I'd love to hear more examples of what this looks like in practice—of what not to do, how to do this badly, and what you think are counterexamples of a PM doing this context sharing really effectively.
turns.zh: 我很想听更多关于这在实践中是什么样子的例子——比如不该做什么、如何做得很糟，以及你认为什么是产品经理非常有效地进行上下文共享的反例。

turns.en: If you think something's more important than something else, ask yourself: why did you conclude that? Reverse engineer your thinking—what made you realize that? And why does the other person you're telling that to—why do they know that? It might be because they don't have the data points, the quantitative or qualitative data that were involved. It might be because they weren't in those meetings or they don't have that information. So you're always thinking about what can I do to bring people along on the journey. The best designers, as a great example, aren't necessarily handing over the designs. They're getting the team to co-create together and explore concepts together. Now they may take that all and then finesse it and bring it out—but when the team's involved in that process, their aha moments completely change. Another example: I had a product manager the other day who's getting every engineer in the team to go and use different AI tools and to come back and tell them what worked and what didn't work for them. And that's something we typically wouldn't do. We'd say, oh the PMs or the designers will go do that, but getting everyone involved in the process is a huge one. We just came out of our annual—biannual—event in Europe with customers. We try to take engineers to the booths and engineers man the booths with me and other people, and they're fronting customers and hearing feedback, and that's ways we can build shared brains together, right? So a lot of that. Now granted, you may start off your project and you take the decisions yourself and you're trying to get things going, but your job always as a PM is: how do I move away from this thing? How do I get better alignment on the vision? They put this on the roadmap and I disagree with it. Why do I disagree with it? Maybe there's some strategic beliefs that I have that I haven't built a shared brain around with the team, or maybe I'm wrong and they're right. So you're always trying to close those gaps. You're always trying to find where the gaps are and then what activities can you do to close those gaps?
turns.zh: 如果你认为某件事比另一件事更重要，问问自己：你为什么得出这个结论？逆向工程你的思考过程——是什么让你意识到这一点？以及你要告诉的那个人——他们为什么知道这一点？可能是因为他们没有那些数据点，那些定量或定性数据。可能是因为他们没参加那些会议，或者他们没有那个信息。所以你总是在想，我能做什么来让人们一起踏上这段旅程。最好的设计师就是一个很好的例子，他们不一定直接交出设计稿，而是让团队一起共同创造、一起探索概念。他们可能会把所有这些拿过来再打磨并呈现出来——但当团队参与那个过程时，他们的顿悟时刻会完全改变。另一个例子：前几天我有一个产品经理，让团队里的每个工程师去使用不同的 AI 工具，然后回来告诉他们哪些有用、哪些没用。这是我们通常不会做的。我们会说，哦，产品经理或设计师会去做那个，但让每个人都参与这个过程是非常重要的。我们刚结束在欧洲与客户的年度——半年度——活动。我们试着带工程师去展台，工程师和我以及其他人在展台服务，他们面对客户并听取反馈，这就是我们一起构建共享大脑的方式，对吧？所以很多这样的做法。当然，你可能在项目开始时自己做决定，试图让事情运转起来，但作为产品经理，你的工作始终是：我如何摆脱这个状态？我如何让愿景更好地对齐？他们把这个放在路线图上，我不同意。我为什么不同意？也许我有一些战略信念，但我还没有和团队建立共享大脑，或者也许我错了而他们是对的。所以你总是在试图缩小这些差距。你总是在寻找差距在哪里，然后你可以做什么活动来缩小这些差距？

turns.en: So interesting. So there's kind of this spectrum that you could think about PMs—of how they operate in different companies. One end of the spectrum: they're the boss, make all the decisions, they are basically managers of the team. The other: they're just completely equal, no additional power of any kind in decision making. Where in that spectrum do you think a PM should be?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。所以你可以想象产品经理在不同公司运作方式的一个光谱。一端是：他们是老板，做所有决定，基本上是团队的管理者。另一端是：他们完全平等，在决策中没有任何额外的权力。你认为产品经理应该在这个光谱的哪个位置？

turns.en: They're always striving to be in the equal—no additional power. Now think about it also in theory: PMs don't have—a PM working in a squad has no reports to them. They have to influence without authority, right? By definition. So there are two operating models here. There is: I will hand over the spec and you will do what the spec says. Or there's the model of: I'm going to get you all aboard into the vision and we're going to work on this together—to the point where the best engineers are almost suggesting their own features to solve the customer problems. Some of the best stuff that we've had—if I share a quick example, I love telling this story because it's an old story and people are like, what? In 2010, I remember interviewing a set of Confluence customers and we could see that—before emoji even existed—customers were putting in these little icons in their Confluence pages, right? And now quantitatively you look at the data and you're like, oh people are putting in these icons, we should ship more icons, give them more variety of icons, whatever. And we particularly found in this one customer call that they would put these red stars and these green stars in their meeting notes in Confluence. And we saw this with multiple customers—like a different system they built—and we're like, why are you doing that? And they'd be like, oh the red stars are the things we haven't done and the green stars are the things we've done. And this engineer at the time left the meeting and she's like, why don't we just put a checkbox in a Confluence page and let them actually tick it? And don't forget—this is 2010, no one had done this on the web. Putting tasks in a document editor was not a concept that existed. And she just pioneered that because of her aha moment from observing the customer. We wouldn't have got that otherwise. Look, there's lots of examples of these, but when they're involved in that journey, you're making them the mini product managers in each of the areas.
turns.zh: 他们总是努力处于平等——没有额外权力的位置。现在也从理论上想想：产品经理没有——在一个小组里工作的产品经理没有下属。他们必须没有权威地施加影响，对吧？从定义上就是这样。所以这里有两种运作模式。一种是：我交出规格说明，你按照规格说明做。另一种模式是：我要让你们所有人都认同愿景，我们一起努力——直到最好的工程师几乎在提出自己的功能来解决客户问题。我们有过的一些最好的东西——如果我分享一个快速的例子，我喜欢讲这个故事，因为这是一个老故事，人们会说，什么？2010 年，我记得采访了一组 Confluence 客户，我们可以看到——甚至在 emoji 存在之前——客户在他们的 Confluence 页面里放这些小图标，对吧？现在从定量上看数据，你会说，哦人们在放这些图标，我们应该发布更多图标，给他们更多种类的图标，等等。我们特别在一次客户电话中发现，他们会在 Confluence 的会议记录里放这些红色星星和绿色星星。我们也在多个客户那里看到了这一点——就像他们构建的一个不同系统——我们问，你们为什么这样做？他们会说，哦红色星星是我们还没做的事情，绿色星星是我们已经做的事情。当时这位工程师离开会议后说，为什么我们不直接在 Confluence 页面里放一个复选框，让他们真正打勾呢？别忘了——这是 2010 年，没人在网上做过这个。在文档编辑器里放任务是一个不存在的概念。她只是因为观察客户而有了顿悟时刻，就开创了这个。否则我们不会得到那个。看，有很多这样的例子，但当他们参与那个旅程时，你就是在让他们成为各个领域的小产品经理。

turns.en: I know you also have this framework of how you think about archetypes of PMs. There's artist PMs, there's a couple others. Talk about that because I think a lot of people—they hear PM and it's like one type of person, and it turns out you can be a successful PM in different ways. Talk about this framework.
turns.zh: 我知道你还有一个关于产品经理原型的框架。有艺术家型产品经理，还有几个其他的。谈谈这个吧，因为我认为很多人——他们听到产品经理就觉得是某一种人，而事实证明你可以用不同的方式成为成功的产品经理。谈谈这个框架。

turns.en: Yeah, we have a framework that Geoff Redfern actually created when he joined us. He shared it with me and we've stuck with it since. You know, there's different types of PM frameworks out there. I think if you pick one and stick with one, it's useful.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有一个框架，实际上是 Geoff Redfern 加入我们时创建的。他和我分享了它，我们一直沿用至今。你知道，市面上有不同的产品经理框架。我认为如果你选一个并坚持用下去，它是有用的。

turns.en: But he has what we call the PM craft triangle. One side of the triangle he has a general manager, other side he has a scientist, and the other side he has an artist. And the positions of the triangle represent how you might do product discovery more naturally. So as an example, a scientist PM will be very hypothesis driven. Think of them in growth teams, think of them as A/B testing a lot, etc. General manager PM will think more in TAM and business and profit and revenue and all that kind of stuff. And an artist PM will be more just emotionally vision led and experience led. And I found this to be a helpful framework because the classic 'let's just throw a PM in a team' isn't the right thing to do. It's like don't throw bodies at the problem. Think about what type of PM are we after and how can we best map that PM. So we use that a lot in calibration when we're comparing PMs. We use that a lot in hiring. Like you'll ask a general question like what's your favorite product and what will you do to make it better. You can tell someone's where they sit in the triangle by how they answer it. Like the make it better answers for the general managers often like there's a new business opportunity we should go after and I think the TAM is this big and I'm going to measure it and whatever. And the scientists will start with a hypothesis and they'll be like oh we could test these different variants etc. And the artists will just paint some visual vision and then kind of back their way into what the problems are. But they'll start with like this solution experience that they want to paint because they feel emotionally led towards that destination for a particular reason, their intuition, their usage or whatever and they'll look backwards. So you can do that. So it's a very helpful tool to say oh we need a new PM on this team and I'm like oh what kind of work are we looking at and do we need more of an artist, a scientist, a general manager. You get some PMs that say I'd like to do all three. The reality is I have found very few people in my career that can do all three really well. But you can get a lot of people who can do all three at a basic level and they're awesome for zero to one projects, startups etc. Like you need just do whatever you need to do to get to the outcome. You need that culture a lot in smaller zero to one projects or startup teams. The bigger you get the more you have the luxury of being like we need someone just to really focus on the growth metrics of this particular product and this particular area or etc.
turns.zh: 但他有一个我们称之为 PM 能力三角的框架。三角形的一边是总经理型，另一边是科学家型，还有一边是艺术家型。三角形中的位置代表了你在产品发现时更自然的方式。举个例子，科学家型的 PM 会非常注重假设驱动。可以想象他们在增长团队中，经常做 A/B 测试等等。总经理型的 PM 会更关注 TAM、业务、利润、收入和这类东西。而艺术家型的 PM 更偏向情感驱动的愿景和体验。我发现这是一个很有用的框架，因为传统的‘随便往团队里塞一个 PM’并不是正确的做法。这就像不要往问题上堆人力。要思考我们需要什么类型的 PM，以及如何最好地匹配那个 PM。所以我们在校准 PM 时经常用这个框架。在招聘中也经常用。比如你会问一个通用的问题：你最喜欢的产品是什么，你会怎么改进它。通过他们的回答你就能看出他们在三角形中的位置。对于总经理型的人来说，改进的答案往往是：有一个新的商业机会我们应该去追求，我认为 TAM 有这么大，我要去衡量它等等。科学家型的人会从假设开始，他们会说我们可以测试这些不同的变体等等。而艺术家型的人会先描绘一些视觉愿景，然后倒推问题是什么。但他们开始于他们想要描绘的解决方案体验，因为他们出于某种原因、直觉、使用习惯等情感上被那个目的地所引导，然后他们会往回看。所以你可以这样做。这是一个非常有用的工具，当你说哦我们团队需要一个新 PM，我就会问哦我们要看的是什么类型的工作，我们需要更多艺术家型、科学家型还是总经理型。有些 PM 会说我想三者都做。现实是，在我的职业生涯中我发现很少有人能真正做好这三者。但你可以找到很多能在基础层面上做到三者的人，他们非常适合从 0 到 1 的项目、初创公司等。就像你需要做任何你需要做的事情来达到结果。在较小的从 0 到 1 的项目或初创团队中，你非常需要这种文化。公司越大，你就越有奢侈去说我们需要一个人真正专注于这个特定产品或这个特定领域的增长指标等等。

turns.en: What I love about this... there's a bunch of reasons. One is it shows you you can be successful in different ways and you don't have to be one specific type of PM. Two is this explains why you may be suffering and failing right now is you may be the wrong kind of PM for the team you're on now.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个框架的原因有很多。一是它表明你可以通过不同的方式取得成功，你不必是某一种特定类型的 PM。二是它解释了为什么你现在可能感到痛苦和失败：你可能不适合你现在的团队。

turns.en: Lenny, the amount of times I've had someone who may not be finding their groove in a particular project, swapping the type of project they're on and they've bounced back, got a new found energy. I can point to so many examples that it happens all the time. And it's a classic of like just find the work that's most suitable to that person and it's not about just throwing PM bodies at the problem. It's just about who would have thought diverse teams still matter. What kind of person do we need in this team? How do they complement the other people? What's the kind of work? And you kind of map that there.
turns.zh: Lenny，我遇到过很多次，有人在某个项目中找不到状态，换了一个项目类型后就反弹了，重新获得了能量。我可以举出很多例子，这种情况经常发生。这就是典型的：找到最适合那个人的工作，而不是往问题上堆 PM 人力。这就是关于谁曾想到多元化团队仍然重要。我们需要什么样的人加入这个团队？他们如何与其他人互补？工作类型是什么？然后你就在那里进行映射。

turns.en: I know that you also have this and I share this philosophy that you don't need to be great at everything and just as an employee and as a PM as well that you don't need to be great at everything. Instead, figure out what you're strong at and focus on that. And it connects to this framework. Talk about just that and I think it's just this kind of myth you think a lot of people believe.
turns.zh: 我知道你也有这个观点，我也认同这个理念：你不需要事事都擅长，作为员工和 PM 也是如此，你不需要事事都擅长。相反，找出你的强项并专注于它。这与这个框架相关。谈谈这个吧，我认为这是很多人相信的一个误区。

turns.en: Yeah, it's also selfishly Lenny, it makes me feel good. So the running joke at Atlassian is I'm like the worst general manager type person to ever have. Like if it's about running the business, don't give that to Sharif. Now, I'm in the exec team, I'm the head of AI, I run the product craft. And I love that people can joke about that about me because I think what that does Lenny is it creates a safe space for other people to be okay to share their weaknesses. And then here's the challenge people run into when they run into a weakness. They have two options. They could try to get better at that thing. Now, sometimes that's left brain, right brain stuff and they might need to work harder at one thing than it is, you know, nature versus nurture kind of topic. Or what I have found to be more useful in my career and I've tried to be the 'I'll get better at that thing', is actually find the thing you're good at and run for the heels towards that direction and ignore everything else. And then build a diverse team around you that's good at the other things. So, I am a very heavy strong artist PM, but I'm responsible for AI across Atlassian. I have a complement Jamille, he works with me. He is the complete opposite of me and we are such a good team together and I'm so grateful for him because in my weaknesses he shines and his weaknesses I shine, but together we're an awesome team. And so I always say if you're early on in your career, try as many things as you can to discover like we discover products, we do product discovery, you should do career discovery. Discover what you're naturally good at. Then you have two options, balance it out or just keep running towards the thing you're naturally good at. My recommendation is always run to the thing towards you're naturally good at, celebrate your weaknesses publicly so that you can build a complementary team around you and create a safe space for everyone else to feel like they can share the same.
turns.zh: 是的，Lenny，自私地说，这让我感觉很好。所以在 Atlassian 有一个常开的玩笑：我是有史以来最糟糕的总经理型的人。就像如果涉及经营业务，别交给 Sharif。现在，我在高管团队，我是 AI 负责人，我负责产品工艺。我喜欢人们可以拿这个开玩笑，因为我认为这创造了一个安全的空间，让其他人可以坦然分享自己的弱点。然后人们遇到弱点时会面临的挑战是：他们有两个选择。他们可以尝试在那个方面变得更好。有时这是左脑右脑的事情，他们可能需要在一个事情上更努力，你知道，是天性还是培养的话题。或者我在职业生涯中发现更有用的是——我试过成为‘我会在那个事情上变得更好’的人——实际上是找到你擅长的事情，朝着那个方向全力奔跑，忽略其他一切。然后在你周围建立一个擅长其他事情的多元化团队。所以，我是一个非常强烈的艺术家型 PM，但我负责 Atlassian 的 AI。我有一个互补的搭档 Jamille，他和我一起工作。他和我完全相反，我们在一起是一个非常好的团队，我非常感激他，因为在我的弱点上他闪耀，在他的弱点上我闪耀，但在一起我们是一个很棒的团队。所以我总是说，如果你处于职业生涯早期，尽可能多地尝试，就像我们发现产品、做产品发现一样，你应该做职业发现。发现你天生擅长什么。然后你有两个选择：平衡它，或者继续朝着你天生擅长的事情奔跑。我的建议总是朝着你天生擅长的事情奔跑，公开庆祝你的弱点，这样你就可以在你周围建立一个互补的团队，并为其他人创造一个安全的空间，让他们觉得他们也可以分享同样的东西。

turns.en: I believe it's important to say you don't you can be terrible at things like you there's probably a baseline. You have to be good enough at meetings, good enough at strategy, good enough at artist at taste at but you don't need to be the best at every category.
turns.zh: 我认为重要的是要说，你可以在某些事情上很糟糕，但可能有一个基线。你必须在会议中足够好，在战略上足够好，在艺术品味上足够好，但你不需要在每个类别中都做到最好。

turns.en: Correct. Yeah, I think it's the again one of those misconceptions that like everyone wants to be Steve Jobs esque kind of like I'm good at everything etc. Now lady don't get me wrong, there are a couple people in the company like I would use Mike our CEO co-founder as an example. He will be in a strategy review with you and he'll tell you why your drop shadows are off by five pixels, why the padding and margins are off on the left here.
turns.zh: 没错。是的，我认为这又是一个误解，就像每个人都想成为史蒂夫·乔布斯那种‘我什么都擅长’的人。但女士，别误会我的意思，公司里有几个人，比如我们的 CEO 联合创始人 Mike。他会和你一起进行战略审查，他会告诉你为什么你的投影阴影偏了五个像素，为什么左边的内边距和外边距不对。

turns.en: Then he'll go tell you why your business model's completely wrong, flip it around, and then he'll look at the data inside out and tell you something you had no idea about. Those people are incredibly hard to find, but the vast majority of folks, I think, find the area they're good at and just keep going in that area.
turns.zh: 然后他会告诉你，你的商业模式完全错了，把它彻底翻过来，接着他会把数据翻个底朝天，告诉你一些你完全没想到的事。这种人极其难找，但我认为绝大多数人都是找到自己擅长的领域，然后就在那个领域里一直做下去。

turns.en: Let me ask you this. When you coach people in their early career and then in later career, if you had to pick one or two of the most common unlocks that help them accelerate — say you're coaching someone early career — think about the people you've helped at the beginning of their career, and then the second part is just later career. What are the most common unlocks that allow them to all of a sudden become a lot more successful at product management?
turns.zh: 我想问你这个问题。当你辅导处于职业早期的人，以及职业后期的人时，如果只能挑一两个最常见的、能帮他们加速成长的“解锁点”——比如你在辅导一个职业早期的人——想想你在他们职业初期帮助过的人，第二部分就是职业后期。最常见的、能让他们突然在产品管理上成功得多的解锁点是什么？

turns.en: Giving them an opportunity that is just above their level at the right time is key. And that opportunity you should be very deliberate about. It's something that plays to their strengths specifically. For example, this product manager comes to mind — she used to work with me in the early days of a new product that we launched a few years ago at Atlassian. And I realized at the time that she was at the stage where she was more in the scientist brain, and the product was growing. And I realized also that I'm probably not the best to lead this, and I stepped aside and just said, hey, Rachel, you should probably take over this piece of work. So I think it's really about finding — if you know where each person is at on their journey, and you can see where they want to head and what they're good at — waiting for the right opportunity. Your job as a leader is to see that opportunity arise and then, you know, move them across to a different team or whatever it is. I think that is the sweet spot of giving people something. I've been fortunate to be here 17 years, and every time I've looked around, there's a new opportunity at Atlassian. This is because we've just grown so much. And these opportunities have happened to play to my strengths. So in the same token, I need to be looking at that for the people on my team and passing that on as well. So I think that's key — just identifying opportunities inside the business is such an important thing that doesn't get talked about as much here.
turns.zh: 在合适的时机给他们一个略高于他们水平的机会，这是关键。而且这个机会你要非常刻意地去设计，它要特别能发挥他们的优势。举个例子，我想到一位产品经理——几年前我们在 Atlassian 推出一款新产品时，她在早期和我一起工作。我当时意识到，她正处在更偏“科学家思维”的阶段，而产品正在成长。我也意识到，我可能不是领导这件事的最佳人选，于是我退到一边，直接说：嘿，Rachel，这块工作也许该由你来接手。所以我认为关键就在于——如果你了解每个人处在旅程的哪个阶段，能看到他们想往哪走、擅长什么——然后等待合适的时机。作为领导者，你的工作就是看到那个机会出现，然后把他们调到别的团队或做别的安排。我觉得这才是给人机会的最佳平衡点。我很幸运在这里待了 17 年，每次我环顾四周，Atlassian 都有新机会。这是因为我们成长得太快了。而这些机会恰好都能发挥我的优势。所以同样地，我也需要为团队里的人寻找这样的机会，并把它传递下去。所以我认为关键就是——在业务内部识别机会，这件事非常重要，但在这里被谈得没那么多。

turns.en: So say an early-career PM is listening to this. They're going to be wondering, okay, what kind of opportunity should I be looking for that is most likely to help my career? What are the signs that this is a good opportunity that may accelerate their career?
turns.zh: 假设一个职业早期的产品经理在听这期节目。他们会想：好吧，我该寻找什么样的机会，才最有可能帮助我的职业发展？有哪些迹象表明这是一个能加速我职业发展的好机会？

turns.en: It probably starts with someone telling you you did a good job at something. That's probably a good sign that that's the type of work that you're good at. So if you're feeling like you've found that and people are saying, you know, they really like the thing I did here, this particular project, they really love how I led growth in this particular area, or they love how I solved this customer problem in this area — analyze that type of project and ask yourself, how did I approach it? How did it work? Then your next thing is: what other types of projects that are similar can I go do? That's what you should be looking at. Tell your manager about it. I always say to folks, a good conversation to have with your manager is to pull up one of those frameworks — like, here's where I think I am in the triangle, whatever framework you want, there are lots of them out there. I'd love to do more of this stuff if you're still discovering, or I would love to get better at the thing I'm good at here. Tell them, indicate to them that you're after the next opportunity. I think it's a huge step you can take to help yourself.
turns.zh: 它很可能始于有人告诉你，你在某件事上做得很好。这很可能就是一个好迹象，说明那就是你擅长的那类工作。所以如果你觉得你找到了它，而且人们在说：他们真的很喜欢我在这里做的事、这个特定的项目，他们很喜欢我在这个领域推动增长的方式，或者他们喜欢我在这个领域解决这个客户问题的方式——那就分析那类项目，问自己：我是怎么着手做的？它是怎么奏效的？然后你的下一步就是：我还能去做哪些类似的项目？这才是你应该关注的。把它告诉你的经理。我总是跟大家说，和经理的一次好对话，就是拿出一个框架——比如“我认为我在这个三角里处于这个位置”，随便你用什么框架，市面上有很多。如果你还在探索，就说我很想多做这类事；或者我很想在我擅长的这件事上变得更好。告诉他们，向他们表明你在追求下一个机会。我认为这是你能为自己做的一大步。

turns.en: What about, let's say, a senior PM — you know, I don't know, like L6 or even an early manager? What's the most common unlock that accelerates their career from that point?
turns.zh: 那比如说一位资深产品经理——我也不确定，比如 L6，甚至是刚做管理的人？从那个阶段开始，最常见的、能加速他们职业发展的解锁点是什么？

turns.en: I think at an L6 you've really found your groove. So I think you're at that decision where maybe you don't want to accelerate — if by accelerate career you mean accelerate your levels. Maybe you want to go diverse, as in go try something totally different. You could argue, is that accelerating your career? I would still say that's accelerating your career, right? Or just keep chasing the similar type of work. I think it's key. This particular lady in one of my teams — yesterday we celebrated her 10-year anniversary at Atlassian. She found the kind of work that she's really good at. She leads a lot of our pricing and packaging work across AI and all that kind of stuff, and she's so good at it. And she just keeps finding more work across the business that lines up with that. So she's chasing that kind of work because she knows she does such a good job with that stuff.
turns.zh: 我认为到了 L6，你其实已经找到了自己的节奏。所以我觉得你处在一个需要做决定的节点：也许你并不想“加速”——如果你说的加速职业是指加速晋升层级的话。也许你想走多元化路线，去尝试完全不同的东西。你可能会争论，那算不算加速职业？我仍然会说那是在加速你的职业，对吧？或者就是继续做类似类型的工作。我认为这很关键。我团队里有一位女士——昨天我们庆祝了她在 Atlassian 的十周年。她找到了自己真正擅长的那类工作。她负责我们很多定价和打包方面的工作，涉及 AI 之类的，她非常擅长。而且她不断在业务中找到更多与之相符的工作。所以她在追求那类工作，因为她知道自己在这方面做得非常好。

ts.sec: Why PMs are thriving in the AI era

turns.en: Okay. I want to talk about something that's hot off the presses. I haven't shared this with anyone yet. I think this will be out by the time this episode comes out. I'm doing a state of the tech job market report. I do this a couple times a year. I've done it maybe three times now, where we basically look at hiring trends across tech and we look at PM, engineering, design, things like that. One of the most interesting takeaways right now — that I hope is out there by the time this is out — is that PMs seem to be benefiting most in the AI era. We are seeing the most open PM roles of any role. Engineering is actually slowing down open engineering roles. Design is very flat, not looking great. User research — really not great. There are a hundred open roles for user research globally at tech companies right now. A hundred and eight. So interestingly, when AI became a thing, many people were like, PMs are over. We don't need them. Why do we need them? Get rid of them. Surprisingly, it's the role that seems to be most thriving right now. And I actually had a post about this where I predicted this. I feel really good about this. So let me ask you this: why do you think this is the case? Why do you think PMs are doing so well in the AI era?
turns.zh: 好。我想聊一个刚刚出炉的东西。我还没跟任何人分享过。我想等这期节目播出时它应该已经发布了。我在做一份科技就业市场状况报告。我一年做几次，到现在大概做了三次，基本上就是看整个科技行业的招聘趋势，看产品、工程、设计这些岗位。目前最有意思的发现之一——我希望播出时它已经发布了——是产品经理似乎在 AI 时代受益最多。我们看到产品经理的开放岗位是所有岗位里最多的。工程岗位实际上在放缓。设计非常平，看起来不太好。用户研究——真的不太好。现在全球科技公司只有一百个用户研究的开放岗位。一百零八个。所以有意思的是，当 AI 兴起时，很多人说产品经理完蛋了，我们不需要他们了，为什么要他们？把他们裁掉。但出乎意料的是，这似乎是目前最兴旺的岗位。我其实发过一篇帖子预测了这一点。我对此感觉很好。所以我想问你：你认为为什么会这样？你觉得为什么产品经理在 AI 时代表现这么好？

turns.en: I think for a while — if I could use a misconception I've been trying to debunk for a while, especially even with our customers and inside Atlassian; I wrote a post about it — but I think for a while, especially a year ago, it felt like the narrative was everyone's becoming an AI builder. Everyone. And if the definition of an AI builder here, to make it more useful, is someone who spends most of their time building software with AI — and an AI builder is all you need, and the roles are merging into one, etc. If I could share a case study, I think that adds to one of your data points inside Atlassian.
turns.zh: 我认为有一段时间——如果我可以提一个我一直试图破除的误解，尤其是在我们的客户和 Atlassian 内部；我为此写过一篇帖子——但我觉得有一段时间，尤其是一年前，叙事好像是每个人都在变成 AI 构建者。每个人。而如果这里把 AI 构建者定义得更有用一点，就是那种把大部分时间花在用 AI 构建软件上的人——而且你只需要 AI 构建者，各种角色正在合并成一个，等等。如果我可以分享一个案例研究，我觉得它能补充你其中一个数据点，就在 Atlassian 内部。

turns.en: So what we did was we were like, okay, maybe this is where it's headed. Let's look at it as a craft. Let's try to create a few squads that have AI builders, and we moved some of our product managers and designers to a few teams that ran these experiments—basically built product where everyone was the AI builder. There was no PM or designer, but they came from different crafts.
turns.zh: 所以我们当时想，好吧，也许这就是未来的方向。让我们把它看作一门手艺。我们试着组建几个拥有 AI 构建者的团队，把一些产品经理和设计师调到几个团队去跑这些实验——基本上就是构建产品，每个人都是 AI 构建者。没有产品经理或设计师，但他们来自不同的专业领域。

turns.en: I remember checking in with one of the PMs in one of the teams, in one of our one-on-ones in the first few weeks, and he's like, 'It's unbelievable, man. You're constantly building. It's so good. I feel like we've moved so fast. We've moved faster than ever before, you know, early days.' It was just amazing.
turns.zh: 我记得在头几周的一次一对一沟通中，我和其中一个团队的产品经理聊了聊，他说：‘太不可思议了，老兄。你一直在构建。感觉太好了。我觉得我们进展得非常快。我们比以往任何时候都快，你知道，早期的时候。’真是太棒了。

turns.en: Yeah, everyone's going to be an AI builder.
turns.zh: 是啊，每个人都会成为 AI 构建者。

turns.en: I'm like, wow, really? Is that where it's going to hit? After about a month he comes back and he's like, 'Everyone's gone back to doing their traditional jobs.' I'm like, 'What? Sorry, what do you mean by that?' He's like, 'It sounds so obvious in hindsight. We realize throughput's not our problem. Direction is our problem. But throughput's getting cheaper.'
turns.zh: 我心想，哇，真的吗？这就是未来的趋势吗？大约一个月后，他回来说：‘大家都回去做传统工作了。’我说：‘什么？抱歉，你什么意思？’他说：‘事后看来太明显了。我们意识到吞吐量不是我们的问题。方向才是我们的问题。但吞吐量越来越便宜了。’

turns.en: So I wrote this blog post internally that was, you know, 'Direct the ship, don't row it.' And there was a lot of PMs coming to us saying, 'Should I be coding? Do I need to code?' And quite a few of our PMs have committed code in some capacity or whatever. But it's very obvious in a world where—again, the new ones here is—if you're a startup and everyone's moving really fast, everyone needs to do anything, which I'm fully poured into that, or a zero-to-one project. In an engineering company where you have the luxury of hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands of engineers—dozens of engineers—your problem is your direction, not how quick you can pump things out.
turns.zh: 所以我在内部写了一篇博客文章，叫做‘指引航向，而不是划桨。’有很多产品经理来找我们问：‘我应该写代码吗？我需要写代码吗？’我们有不少产品经理以某种方式提交过代码。但很明显，在一个——再说一次，这里的新情况是——如果你是一家初创公司，每个人都在快速行动，每个人都需要做任何事，我完全投入其中，或者是一个从零到一的项目。在一家工程公司，你有幸拥有数百、数千、数万名工程师——几十名工程师——你的问题是方向，而不是你能多快地产出东西。

turns.en: So people who are actually helping everyone steer the ship, not more throughput, right? So I think that probably is in support of that, Lenny. I think more people are raising—there's more throughput, so I need more people to steer the ship. This is probably reflective of some of the results you're seeing on more PMs being hired.
turns.zh: 所以真正帮助大家指引航向的人，而不是更多的吞吐量，对吧？所以我认为这 probably 支持了这一点，Lenny。我认为更多人在提升——有更多吞吐量，所以我需要更多人来指引航向。这 probably 反映了你看到的一些关于招聘更多产品经理的结果。

turns.en: That is an awesome answer. And that makes—I imagine so many people hearing this are just nodding along.
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的回答。这让我想象到很多人听到这个都会点头赞同。

turns.en: Yes, this is exactly right in spite of what we keep hearing—PMs should be shipping code, PMs should be building. There's a few directions I want to go here. I guess just to double down on what you're saying: what AI is enabling is anyone can build, which is creating a ton of chaos and a lot of prototypes and a lot of ideas. And what you're seeing here with this data is probably showing is now the need is, what the hell are we actually doing? Let's all get on the same page. It's like more buying. We need more buying. We need more alignment. We need all the things PMs are great at. Also, what is great? Is this ready? Is this good? Is this what we want? Is this going to hit our goals? So it's like now that we think about it, I see this makes all the sense. Here's why we need more PMs. It's so interesting that we thought the opposite would happen.
turns.zh: 是的，这完全正确，尽管我们不断听到产品经理应该写代码、产品经理应该构建。这里我想往几个方向聊。我想就你说的再深入一点：AI 所赋能的是任何人都能构建，这创造了大量混乱、大量原型和大量想法。而你在这里看到的数据 probably 表明，现在的需求是，我们到底在做什么？让我们达成共识。这就像更多的购买。我们需要更多的购买。我们需要更多的对齐。我们需要产品经理擅长的所有事情。还有，什么是好的？这准备好了吗？这好吗？这是我们要的吗？这能实现我们的目标吗？所以现在想想，我觉得这完全合理。这就是为什么我们需要更多产品经理。有趣的是我们以为会发生相反的情况。

turns.en: And we thought the same thing would happen with other crafts, Mert. I mean—
turns.zh: 我们以为其他专业领域也会发生同样的事情，Mert。我是说——

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Lenny, you were probably around—I'm guessing your age, Lenny, so no offense—you're probably around during the Balsamiq mockup era, right?
turns.zh: Lenny，你 probably 经历过——我猜你的年龄，Lenny，所以无意冒犯——你 probably 经历过 Balsamiq 原型图时代，对吧？

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.en: So like, you know, what was the promise there? Everyone can do mockups. Mockups are so easy, right? Let's just ignore AI prototyping. And Atlassian—yeah, Balsamiq exploded and we used a whole bunch of mockup tools and it was 'we liberate mockups.' I learned so much through that era at Atlassian. I learned that one, yeah, everyone can create a prototype or a mockup. But yeah, actually PMs are some of the worst solution designers in the world. Like, you realize—because you have access to the tool doesn't mean you're an expert at the domain that you have access to, right? So like now some PMs, more the artistic ones, end up doing just generally better mockups than others. So AI is really good at amplifying your strengths and equally it amplifies your weaknesses.
turns.zh: 那么，你知道，当时的承诺是什么？每个人都能做原型图。原型图太简单了，对吧？让我们暂时忽略 AI 原型设计。Atlassian——是的，Balsamiq 爆炸式增长，我们使用了一大堆原型图工具，口号是‘我们解放原型图。’我在 Atlassian 的那个时代学到了很多。我学到的一点是，是的，每个人都能创建原型或原型图。但实际上，产品经理是世界上最差的解决方案设计师之一。就像你意识到——因为你有工具的使用权，并不意味着你是你所接触领域的专家，对吧？所以现在一些产品经理，更有艺术感的那部分，通常比其他人做出更好的原型图。所以 AI 非常擅长放大你的优势，同样也放大你的弱点。

turns.en: So we learned there in that world that specialists are still important and specialization is still important. Like you can only get the AI to do something as good as your knowledge of the specialization is, if that makes sense. Because you've got to learn how to prompt it. We saw it with the mockups era and now we're seeing it again with the prototypes era and everyone can generate a prototype. It's awesome. I mean it certainly helps speed up decision making and all that stuff, but it's a fly in the world with like all PMs and our designers. Like it's yes, everyone's circles are getting bigger. Like think of it as a Venn diagram, but the circles aren't overlapping. It's just they're all equally getting bigger. So if they're equally getting bigger, then they're not compressing, if that makes sense. The specializations are still needed to improve the quality and taste that's coming out of each of those things. Yeah, that's just often missed as well, I think, that whole topic.
turns.zh: 所以我们在那个世界学到，专家仍然重要，专业化仍然重要。就像你只能让 AI 做到与你对专业化的知识一样好，如果这说得通的话。因为你必须学会如何提示它。我们在原型图时代看到了这一点，现在在原型时代又看到了，每个人都能生成原型。这很棒。我的意思是，这确实有助于加速决策等等，但这对所有产品经理和我们的设计师来说是个难题。就像是的，每个人的圈子都在变大。把它想象成维恩图，但圆圈并不重叠。只是它们都在同等变大。所以如果它们同等变大，那么它们就没有压缩，如果这说得通的话。专业化仍然需要来提高每个领域产出的质量和品味。是的，这经常被忽视，我认为，整个话题。

turns.en: I love this. Okay. So again, this is a fun spectrum. On one end of the spectrum of what a PM should be doing, on one end, you are now an engineer. You're shipping production. This is part of your job now. The other end is don't even touch AI at all. Just do what you used to do. Like you actually spend a lot of time thinking about career ladders and calibration and what a great PM should—what a successful PM looks like. So this is something you spend a lot of time on. Which—what do you think a PM should be doing in terms of AI infusing their job, prototyping, I imagine. Should they be shipping code? What do you think is the right answer for PMs these days?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。好的。所以再次，这是一个有趣的谱系。在产品经理应该做什么的谱系的一端，你现在是一名工程师。你在发布生产代码。这是你现在工作的一部分。另一端是根本不碰 AI。就做你以前做的事。你实际上花了很多时间思考职业阶梯和校准，以及一个伟大的产品经理应该——一个成功的产品经理是什么样子。所以这是你花很多时间的事情。那么——你认为产品经理在 AI 融入工作方面应该做什么，原型设计，我想。他们应该写代码吗？你认为现在产品经理的正确答案是什么？

turns.en: I'd tie it back up to the top, Lenny, which is their job is to make sure the team—data and decision making—PMs own decision making velocity. And so they're thinking of how can I help the team move faster? The second question is, oh, can I help me in any of those? I think that's the right mindset. So it's like if I realize that, okay, customer empathy and customer awareness is a huge problem, a context gap my team has, and I just feel like they're not making the right micro decisions because they don't understand this persona over that persona, etc. Then you'll probably be thinking about how can I involve them in the process, but also how can I use AI in the process to accelerate them filling that context gap. I think I would go back to the top and just answer that question of like look at your team today.
turns.zh: 我会把它拉回到最上面，Lenny，也就是他们的工作是确保团队——数据和决策——产品经理拥有决策速度。所以他们在想，我怎样才能帮助团队更快前进？第二个问题是，哦，我能在其中任何方面帮助自己吗？我认为这是正确的心态。所以就像如果我意识到，好吧，客户同理心和客户意识是我团队的一个巨大问题，一个上下文差距，我只是觉得他们没有做出正确的微观决策，因为他们不理解这个角色而不是那个角色，等等。那么你 probably 会思考我怎样才能让他们参与这个过程，同时也如何在这个过程中使用 AI 来加速他们填补那个上下文差距。我想我会回到最上面，就回答那个问题，比如看看你今天的团队。

turns.en: There are some things that you might feel like are not gelling well, and you go, what is the context gap? And then look at how AI can help you do that. Is it because you don't have direction in the vision? So sure, prototyping might help you get a better vision and clarify it and all that kind of stuff. But you might realize that they don't have a good understanding of the market dynamics, and you might send off a bunch of agents to do some analysis and build that with the team, etc. So, first stating the problem with the context gap and then using AI to help solve that, I think is the right approach.
turns.zh: 有些事情你可能觉得不太对劲，然后你会问，上下文差距是什么？接着看看 AI 如何帮你做到这一点。是因为你在愿景上没有方向吗？当然，原型设计可能帮你获得更好的愿景并澄清它等等。但你可能会意识到他们对市场动态没有很好的理解，你可能会派出一堆智能体去做一些分析，并与团队一起构建，等等。所以，首先陈述上下文差距的问题，然后用 AI 来帮助解决它，我认为这是正确的方法。

turns.en: I love that answer. Very unlikely it will be the bottleneck for decision making and shipping code to production. Most likely that is the last thing that you need to speed up because that is so easy now. Unless, as you said, if it's like a startup or just like a new team or it's just a PM, for example, working on something. Okay. Amazing. So, while we're on this topic of AI, you hire a lot of PMs, you interview a lot of PMs. I love asking this question. What's kind of trending up in what you are looking for when you are hiring PMs? What are kind of emerging newer skills, habits, traits? And what's trending down? What's less important now?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个回答。它不太可能成为决策和将代码发布到生产的瓶颈。最可能的是，这是你最不需要加速的事情，因为现在这太容易了。除非，如你所说，如果是初创公司或新团队，或者只是一个 PM 在做某事。好的。太棒了。那么，既然我们在 AI 这个话题上，你招聘很多 PM，面试很多 PM。我喜欢问这个问题。在招聘 PM 时，你寻找的东西中什么在呈上升趋势？有哪些新兴的技能、习惯、特质？什么在呈下降趋势？现在什么不太重要了？

turns.en: Trending up in certainly larger organizations, I would say, again, to be more nuanced in the topic here, is PMs that are certainly more of the artist type. And why that's the case is because taste has become more important than ever before when everyone has access to the same intelligence. I think that's been covered heavily in your podcast, but I think it's certainly people are more leaning towards experience-led PMs. I think that's certainly trending up. The other big thing that's trending up obviously is, you know, if anyone is in an established workforce, as in they have teams that already exist, right? You're asking yourself, how can I reinvent how each member of my team does their job in the world of AI? The problem you have is probably cultural change if you define culture as how work gets done. And so you're looking at one thing I often do with the interviews and the interview process is you're looking at what new culture would this person bring to the team? And that means how can they transform how we work, especially in the world of AI, right? So, asking people how they work with AI is a fascinating question and getting to the deep beyond the like I use it to summarize stuff and whatever and like actually getting to that because you're also looking at cultural ads, you AI natives or AI natives such a relative term because you by the time you kind of But like you're always looking at like what new ways of working can this person bring? So that's probably the second thing.
turns.zh: 在大型组织中，我想说，为了更细致地讨论这个话题，呈上升趋势的是更偏向艺术家类型的 PM。为什么这样呢？因为当每个人都拥有相同的智能时，品味变得比以往任何时候都重要。我认为你的播客已经大量讨论过这一点，但我认为人们确实更倾向于经验驱动的 PM。这肯定是上升趋势。另一个明显的上升趋势是，如果任何人在一个成熟的工作团队中，也就是说他们已经有现成的团队，对吧？你会问自己，在 AI 世界中，我如何重塑团队中每个成员的工作方式？你遇到的问题可能是文化变革，如果你将文化定义为工作如何完成。所以，我在面试和面试过程中经常做的一件事是，看看这个人会给团队带来什么新文化？这意味着他们如何能改变我们的工作方式，尤其是在 AI 世界中，对吧？所以，问人们如何与 AI 协作是一个有趣的问题，并且要深入下去，超越‘我用它来总结东西’之类的表面回答，真正深入探讨，因为你也关注文化增添，你是 AI 原生代或 AI 原生代这个术语很相对，因为当你……但你总是关注这个人能带来什么新的工作方式？所以这可能是第二点。

turns.en: And the third thing, Lenny, I think this is kind of cultural to some of the narrative that's out there is around hiring people that don't know any better except for AI. And this may sound a bit spicy. Maybe their AI slop levels are higher, but they actually didn't grow up with knowing anything else. In particular, I'm talking about juniors here. So one misconception I'm often debunking with a lot of established organizations is you don't need to hire juniors anymore. And I go, why do you say that? And it's because oh well, AI can do that for me, yada yada yada. But also as an organization, what are some of the problems you're having? And often the problem is, well, I have a workforce that needs to transform and learn new different ways of working. And I don't know about you, but it's really hard for me to unlearn the ways I used to work and then learn the new ways of working. That's very hard. It's much easier to grab someone out of college that's basically been cheating in their university assignments or not knowing any better. Or I love using the example of my son, 12-year-old son. He vibe codes his own games. He's gone from scratch like a visual coding language straight to vibe coding. Like he's missed the whole syntax and whatever. He thinks that's normal. Like I'm always blown away when he'll dismiss a model and be like, Dad, this Gemini wasn't that good and blah blah wasn't that good and did this. I'm like, Dude, that would have taken like four days for someone to build. He's like, yeah, whatever. And I'm like, I'm blown away and he's just like, you know. But the long way of saying is I think the third type of person you're after is And I think in particular juniors for established workforces, they bring different ways of working to the team. Now juniors are not great at identifying AI slop because they don't have the domain expertise. But your established team, your existing team, your seniors, your people that are specialized, they can pick AI slop a mile away they know the domain really well. And so you're actually looking at how can I build a complementary team here, a complementary workforce between the juniors and the seniors so they can work together. So I would say that's the third big thing is like we have definitely overindexed on hiring more juniors than seniors because because again our context is we have an established workforce, an established team that are learning to transform how they work, which is every organization in the world. And so you're going what what's what person can I bring in that doesn't know any better? And so we run these like AI builder weeks and they're fascinating weeks, Lenny, because like we just take a week where all the crafts stop and they tinker with AI for a week engineering design etc. At the same time is very important. The juniors or the younger people tend to be like showing all this coolness and like demos and tools whatever and the seniors tend to focus on identifying slop, evals, quality problems etc. Like you just notice that just natural gravity and you're like wow this is diverse teams and diverse teams are still very important in the world of AI.
turns.zh: 第三点，Lenny，我认为这与现有的一些叙事有关，是关于招聘那些除了 AI 之外不知道其他方式的人。这听起来可能有点辛辣。也许他们的 AI 垃圾水平更高，但他们实际上没有在了解其他东西的环境中长大。特别是，我在这里说的是初级员工。我经常与许多成熟组织澄清的一个误解是，你不再需要招聘初级员工了。我问，你为什么这么说？他们说，哦，AI 可以为我做那件事，等等。但作为一个组织，你遇到的一些问题是什么？通常问题是，我有一支需要转型和学习新的不同工作方式的员工队伍。我不知道你怎么样，但对我来说，忘记过去的工作方式然后学习新的工作方式真的很难。那非常难。更容易的是从大学里招一个基本上在大学作业中作弊或不知道更好的人。或者我喜欢用我儿子的例子，12 岁的儿子。他 vibe code 自己的游戏。他从 Scratch 这样的可视化编程语言直接跳到 vibe coding。他错过了整个语法之类的。他认为这很正常。我总是被震惊到，当他贬低一个模型时说，爸爸，这个 Gemini 没那么好，等等没那么好，做了这个。我说，伙计，那需要别人花四天才能构建出来。他说，是啊，随便。而我被震惊到，他只是说，你知道。但长话短说，我认为你想要的第三类人，特别是对于成熟的工作团队，初级员工为团队带来不同的工作方式。现在，初级员工不擅长识别 AI 垃圾，因为他们没有领域专业知识。但你成熟的团队，你现有的团队，你的资深员工，你的专业人员，他们能在一英里外识别 AI 垃圾，他们非常了解领域。所以你实际上是在考虑如何在这里建立一个互补的团队，一个初级和资深之间的互补劳动力，以便他们可以合作。所以我会说这是第三大点，我们肯定过度倾向于招聘更多初级员工而非资深员工，因为再次我们的背景是我们有一个成熟的员工队伍，一个成熟的团队正在学习转变他们的工作方式，这是世界上每个组织都在做的。所以你会问，我能带来什么不知道更好的人？所以我们举办这些 AI 构建者周，它们是非常有趣的周，Lenny，因为我们只是花一周时间，所有的手艺都停下来，他们用 AI 捣鼓一周，工程、设计等。同时非常重要。初级员工或年轻人倾向于展示所有这些酷炫的东西，演示和工具之类的，而资深员工倾向于专注于识别垃圾、评估、质量问题等。你只是注意到这种自然的引力，你会说哇，这是多元化的团队，而多元化的团队在 AI 世界中仍然非常重要。

turns.en: Okay, so on this junior piece, very inspiring. I imagine for folks listening to this that are earlier in their career or trying to get into PM from something else after school, are there any trends of where the best junior/young folks come from college-wise? Like, is it still going to college? Are they studying computer science? Are they MBAs? Anything there?
turns.zh: 好的，关于这个初级产品经理的话题，非常鼓舞人心。我想对于听众中那些职业生涯早期，或者毕业后想从其他领域转行做产品经理的人来说，有没有什么趋势表明最优秀的初级/年轻人才来自哪些大学专业？比如，还是去上大学吗？他们学计算机科学吗？还是 MBA？有什么规律吗？

turns.en: I don't think you have anything unique to share here. I think it's still a mix of computer science. I spoke to our APM cohorts last week in Sydney and we had them all together and it was a mix of there was like some people with arts degrees, someone with a law and technology background. So it was a good mix. Again, you're looking for the critical thinking, the usual stuff, the curiosity is super high, willingness to try different things. They got enough fear. So they're just willing to try anything to try to make it work because they haven't done anything any other way, right? So and we have numbers to show this, Lenny, both internally and externally with our customers, our research team. So like something like almost 30, I think it's 38% posted a blog about it, but like juniors are more likely to adopt new tools than the seniors both internally and with customers etc. On the flip side, the seniors are getting more quality and better productivity out of the ones they're using, but they're less likely to try different ways of working.
turns.zh: 我觉得这里没什么特别的。我认为仍然是计算机科学背景的混合。上周我在悉尼和我们的 APM 学员交流，把他们聚在一起，其中有艺术学位的人，有法律和技术背景的人。所以是个很好的混合。再说，你要找的是批判性思维，那些常见的东西，好奇心超级高，愿意尝试不同的事物。他们无所畏惧。所以他们愿意尝试任何方法去把事情做成，因为他们没有其他方式做过，对吧？我们有数据表明这一点，Lenny，无论是内部还是外部客户，我们的研究团队。所以差不多 30%，我想是 38% 发过一篇博客，但初级员工比高级员工更可能采用新工具，无论是内部还是客户那边等等。反过来，高级员工从他们使用的工具中获得更高质量和更好的生产力，但他们不太愿意尝试不同的工作方式。

turns.en: Okay. So if I were to connect to your three answers of what is trending up: artist PMs, people that bring a culture of open-mindedness and trying stuff and experimentation because things are changing so fast, which feels actually pretty close to the third bucket, which is newer workforce folks that are just AI native essentially. So the Venn diagram is essentially artist PMs who are new juniors, let's say. So going back to the artist PM, say a little bit more what that looks like because people listening to this are going to be wondering, am I that? How do I become that? Talk more about and as one, as you self-describe yourself as what does that look like? What are you graded at as an artist PM?
turns.zh: 好的。所以如果我把你关于趋势的三个回答联系起来：艺术家型产品经理、带来开放思维和尝试与实验文化的人，因为事情变化太快，这实际上感觉非常接近第三个桶，即更年轻的劳动力，本质上是 AI 原生。所以维恩图基本上是艺术家型产品经理中的新初级员工，比如说。那么回到艺术家型产品经理，多说一点那是什么样子，因为听众会想知道，我是那样的人吗？我如何成为那样的人？多谈谈，作为你自己描述的自己，那是什么样子？作为艺术家型产品经理，你被评分的是什么？

turns.en: An artist PM is, in contrast to a general manager or a scientist type of PM, the way they lead product discovery is largely through visions. They may often actually start with solutions and work back into problems, which sounds again very countercultural because they have some intuition in some particular area. They tend to focus on experience more than numerical, you know, more they're more data informed than data driven. Then I want someone in growth to be a little bit more data driven than data informed. You kind of want that healthy tension, right? So they'll tend to do that a lot more. A lot of them will tend to actually a good signal is like you'll see a bunch of prototypes. The artist PM from different PMs, the artist ones will generally do the ones that seem more logical or flow better. You'll find sometimes, I always say when you're in the room and you're discussing a concept or a topic and someone sometimes feels they just pick up the whiteboard marker and draw, that's a pretty good signal that like are we talking about this or are we talking about that? And so often tend to do that. But I think in the world where more vendors and more software is cheaper to build, more people have the same sets of features, experience matters more than ever before and I'm not a believer that everyone's going to chat to an agent and the agent interface is the final interface. I think there'll be many. And so I think experience still matters a lot. So I think that in a world where just generally speaking more people can build more stuff cheaper, faster, easier, experience matters more because that becomes one of your possible differentiators. And so those artists tend to kind of be a better asset, well not a better, a good asset in that world. And so you're trying to complement your workforce to make sure you've got a mix of these skills.
turns.zh: 艺术家型产品经理，与总经理或科学家型产品经理相比，他们领导产品发现的方式主要是通过愿景。他们可能经常从解决方案开始，然后回溯到问题，这听起来又非常反文化，因为他们在某个特定领域有直觉。他们倾向于更关注体验而非数字，你知道，他们更多是数据启发而非数据驱动。而我希望增长团队的人更数据驱动而非数据启发。你需要那种健康的张力，对吧？所以他们倾向于更多地这样做。他们中的许多人倾向于，一个很好的信号是，你会看到一堆原型。来自不同产品经理的艺术家型产品经理，通常会做出那些看起来更合乎逻辑或更流畅的。你会发现有时，我总是说，当你在房间里讨论一个概念或话题时，有人有时觉得他们只是拿起白板笔就画，这是一个很好的信号，表明我们是在谈论这个还是在谈论那个？所以他们经常倾向于这样做。但我认为在一个更多供应商和更多软件构建成本更低的世界里，更多人拥有相同的功能集，体验比以往任何时候都更重要，我不相信每个人都会与智能体聊天，智能体界面是最终界面。我认为会有很多。所以我认为体验仍然很重要。所以我认为在一个普遍来说更多人能更便宜、更快、更容易地构建更多东西的世界里，体验更重要，因为这成为你可能的差异化因素之一。所以那些艺术家往往成为更好的资产，嗯，不是更好，是很好的资产在那个世界里。所以你试图补充你的劳动力，确保你拥有这些技能的混合。

turns.en: I imagine it's hard to actually find that combination of a new entrant into PM and very good at this because my suspicion you need to do this for a while to build that gut feeling and the you know the artist experience. True or not true?
turns.zh: 我想实际上很难找到那种既是产品经理新人又非常擅长这个的组合，因为我怀疑你需要做一段时间才能建立那种直觉和你知道的艺术家经验。真的还是假的？

turns.en: Someone just sent me we asked all our APMs from last cohort the new cohort coming up to record a loom of a take home exercise and I watched a few of them week before last actually and it was fascinating again to see how again they don't have domain experience but we gave them an exercise to build an app for a particular thing and to see how they chose to present it and lead the narrative of why they're building this particular app whatever. You do pick up the artist streak in them very early on. You can see the ones that will as an example there was a loom of someone that went through and they walked through basically graphs before they even got to any experience and they were like here's the business case here's the TAM here's etc whatever whatever and they were like here's experience and they spent very little time on that in contrast to this other candidate and she walked through the end-to-end journey and talked about like it's funny talked about the lighters and like I think this will be a way to build an emotional connection with someone again don't have to don't have any domain experience but you can see the way they tended to do product discovery tends to be more visual than than the than the other person. So you can at least identify that streak early. I mean Lenny I've got two kids my son's really good at maths and logic and whatever and my daughter just loves drawing and just naturally we put them in the same household we read to them the same books as kids at least I think we did but you can just see the natural their preference in their style of how they work and how they think and so I think that there is a bit of nature and nurture here as well.
turns.zh: 有人刚发给我，我们让上一批和即将到来的新一批所有 APM 录制一个回家作业的 loom 视频，我前两周看了几个，很有趣，再次看到他们虽然没有领域经验，但我们给了他们一个练习，为特定事物构建一个应用，看看他们如何选择呈现它并引导为什么构建这个特定应用的叙述。你确实很早就发现他们身上的艺术家特质。你可以看到那些人，举个例子，有一个人的 loom 视频，他们基本上在进入任何体验之前就展示了图表，他们说这是商业案例，这是 TAM，等等等等，然后他们说这是体验，他们在上面花了很少时间，相比之下另一个候选人，她走完了端到端旅程，并谈到，有趣的是谈到打火机，说我认为这将是一种与某人建立情感联系的方式，再次没有领域经验，但你可以看到他们倾向于做产品发现的方式更视觉化，比另一个人更视觉化。所以你至少可以早期识别那种特质。我是说 Lenny，我有两个孩子，我儿子很擅长数学和逻辑什么的，我女儿就是喜欢画画，自然地在同一个家庭里，我们小时候给他们读同样的书，至少我认为我们做了，但你可以看到他们自然的偏好，在他们的工作方式和思维方式上，所以我认为这里有一点天性和教养。

turns.zh: 我还有一个假设，不知道对不对，就是市场还没有越过那个顿悟时刻：体验比什么都重要。我的意思是，在 AI 世界里，也许回溯过去，我们说过所有产品经理有一天都会成为构建者，我想我们正在认识到这绝对不是事实。我认为仍然有一个误解需要被澄清或证明：设计在 AI 世界里比以往任何时候都更重要，因为如果每个人都能获得同样的东西，那么其中一个——或者至少会重要的因素是——

Okay, I like—yeah, I've been feeling the same thing and it's interesting. So your feeling is maybe we're not yet realizing that this is a huge opportunity in the way to differentiate and win.
turns.zh: 哇，我喜欢这个。让我们总结一下：现在就囤积你的设计师，趁没人意识到这是个机会时低价买入。慢一点。把他们和你的备用饮用水一起放在车库里。好吧，我喜欢——是的，我也有同感，这很有趣。所以你的感觉是，也许我们还没有意识到这是一个巨大的机会，是差异化和获胜的方式。
