turns.en: Cool. Okay. I want to go back to a couple of these counter-narratives you mentioned because I think they're really interesting. One that you touched on a bit that I think is worth spending a little more time on, which is not starting with a solution. PMs are constantly told do not start with the solution in mind. Start with the problem, with the customer pain. Don't even talk about the solution yet, all that stuff. Your feeling is that's not actually true in a lot of cases. Talk about what you've experienced, what you've learned there.
turns.zh: 酷。好的。我想回到你提到的几个反叙事，因为我觉得它们真的很有趣。你稍微提到的一个，我认为值得多花点时间，就是不要从解决方案开始。产品经理经常被告知不要从解决方案开始。从问题开始，从客户痛点开始。甚至先不要谈解决方案，所有这些。你的感觉是，在很多情况下这实际上并不正确。谈谈你的经历，你在那里学到了什么。

turns.en: Yeah, I think it's again one of those misconceptions. It's a classic easy thing when you're in a meeting and someone says something and you want to look smart, you'd be like, well, slow down everyone. What's the problem we're trying to solve? And that's like, yo, that person really brought some—
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这又是一个误解。这是一个经典的简单事情：当你在开会时，有人说了一些话，你想显得聪明，你会说，好吧，大家慢点。我们要解决的问题是什么？这就像，哟，那个人真的带来了一些——

turns.en: A step back.
turns.zh: 退一步。

turns.en: Yeah yeah, nice Lenny. You got that one. It's a good question to ask honestly. Yeah, what's the—I think it's still a good question to ask. I just think it is what's not talked about enough is sometimes it's a great way to start with a solution. So a few examples if I could run through them. I think one—sometimes it's okay to start with a solution when you're trying to discover, you feel like there's a hunch in the area, you're trying to discover what the things you could productize are. Maybe some recent examples at Atlassian: we have Rovo, Rovo Chat, which is our AI assistant if you're using our platform, and Rovo Agents. They're agents you can deploy in loops inside Jira workflows, Confluence workflows and so forth. And believe it or not, Lenny, again, three and a half years ago when we created agents in Rovo Chat—three and a half, yeah, geez, AI, it's gone fast. We were debating if we should put these in there because the theory was why would we put like a general chat in there and why would we put agents in there and let people create their own agents? Why don't we productize, like build the feature that people want, don't give them the general canvas, right? So let's not put chat in there, like let's put a summarize button on top of Confluence pages rather than having a chat button to do that. And what you often learn is actually if you give people a canvas, it's sometimes the fastest way to discover what the main problems are and productize some of those problems. So as a simple example, in Confluence whiteboards, customers can draw sticky notes and collaborate with them and whatever, and you know, one of the common scenarios is you might use Rovo Chat to group sticky notes into common themes. Now chat's not—maybe to tie back to our experience discussion—chat is a terrible experience to do that visually, like you're typing, you're kind of like filling out which sticky notes do you want to group into themes? How do you select them? And so obviously you can productize that feature and that team lets you select a bunch of sticky notes and decide, you know, I'm going to group these ones into different themes and AI goes and does that for you. Really good example where you productize the use case the chat had, but chat was the infinite use case. Another example is customers love putting—and we have like nearly 10 million agents that run in loops every month inside Jira and Confluence—and you know, you want to give a ticket to an agent and the agent picks it up and does the triage or agent generates the code or agent reviews the legal contract, whatever it is. That's quite common inside Jira. People put agents in loops. And so we can learn what kinds of agents they're putting in loops and for some of them we're going to leave them as the infinite use case. Let customers build their own. And for some of them we're like, actually we're going to build an AI triage feature and make that native to the product.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，说得好，Lenny。你抓住了那个。老实说，这是一个好问题。是的，什么是——我认为这仍然是一个好问题。我只是认为没有充分讨论的是，有时从解决方案开始是一个很好的方式。所以如果我可以举几个例子。我认为一个——有时当你试图发现时，从解决方案开始是可以的，你觉得在这个领域有一种直觉，你试图发现你可以产品化的东西是什么。也许 Atlassian 最近的一些例子：我们有 Rovo，Rovo Chat，这是我们的 AI 助手，如果你在使用我们的平台，还有 Rovo Agents。它们是你可以部署在 Jira 工作流、Confluence 工作流等内部循环中的智能体。信不信由你，Lenny，又是三年半前，当我们在 Rovo Chat 中创建智能体时——三年半，是的，天哪，AI，发展得太快了。我们在争论是否应该把这些放进去，因为理论是为什么我们要在那里放一个通用聊天，为什么我们要在那里放智能体并让人们创建自己的智能体？为什么我们不产品化，比如构建人们想要的功能，不要给他们通用画布，对吧？所以让我们不要在那里放聊天，比如让我们在 Confluence 页面顶部放一个摘要按钮，而不是有一个聊天按钮来做这件事。而你经常学到的是，实际上如果你给人们一个画布，有时这是发现主要问题并产品化其中一些问题的最快方式。所以作为一个简单的例子，在 Confluence 白板中，客户可以画便利贴并与之协作等等，你知道，一个常见的场景是你可能使用 Rovo Chat 将便利贴分组到共同主题中。现在聊天不是——也许回到我们关于体验的讨论——聊天在视觉上做这件事是一种糟糕的体验，就像你在打字，你有点像是在填写你想把哪些便利贴分组到主题中？你如何选择它们？所以显然你可以产品化那个功能，那个团队让你选择一堆便利贴并决定，你知道，我要把这些分组到不同的主题中，AI 会为你做这件事。非常好的例子，你产品化了聊天所具有的用例，但聊天是无限用例。另一个例子是客户喜欢把——我们每月在 Jira 和 Confluence 内有近 1000 万个智能体在循环中运行——你知道，你想把一张工单交给一个智能体，智能体接手工单并进行分类，或者智能体生成代码，或者智能体审查法律合同，无论是什么。这在 Jira 内非常常见。人们把智能体放在循环中。所以我们可以了解他们在循环中放入什么样的智能体，对于其中一些，我们将把它们保留为无限用例。让客户构建自己的。对于其中一些，我们会说，实际上我们将构建一个 AI 分类功能并使其成为产品的原生功能。

turns.en: And so starting with the customer solution and understanding what the customer is doing helps you work out what the problems are, and then you might productize their manual workaround into a set of capabilities into your product. It's a pretty common tactic. I think I've heard some people refer to it as paving the cow path. Like, you know, there's a walkway and there's a cow that walks straight in the middle across the grass, and you're like, well, why don't we just make that the cow path? And so starting with a customer solution there is a really good approach.
turns.zh: 所以，从客户解决方案出发，理解客户在做什么，能帮你找出问题所在，然后你可以把他们手动变通的方法产品化，变成你产品中的一组能力。这是一种很常见的策略。我听过有人把这叫做“铺牛道”。就像，你知道，有一条走道，有一头牛径直穿过草地中间，然后你说，为什么不干脆把那儿做成牛道呢？所以从客户解决方案出发是一个非常好的方法。

turns.en: The second big one really is product strategy. The best product strategies start by looking at what assets, what solutions do you already have today? Because you need to answer where do we play and how do we win? And to answer how do we win you have to look at what unique things we have as a company, as a business, as a product, right? So the classic example I love to give people is the Amazon bookstore. Who built this ridiculously sized bookstore? It's a huge inventory. If you read Bezos's book, it's like, what other things need a ridiculously large inventory at a crazy scale? Oh, what if it was an everything store? Do you know what I mean? So starting with a solution for product strategy thinking is another good tactic.
turns.zh: 第二个重要的方法其实是产品战略。最好的产品战略始于审视你今天已经拥有哪些资产、哪些解决方案。因为你需要回答：我们在哪里竞争，以及我们如何取胜？而要回答如何取胜，你就必须审视作为一家公司、一项业务、一个产品，我们有哪些独特的东西，对吧？我特别喜欢举的经典例子是亚马逊书店。谁建了那个规模大得离谱的书店？库存巨大。如果你读贝索斯的书，就会想，还有什么其他东西需要规模大得离谱的库存？哦，如果它是一家万物商店呢？你明白我的意思吗？所以从解决方案出发进行产品战略思考是另一个好策略。

turns.en: I said to teams: write down what assets you have today, then write down your beliefs, and see if there's any connection between those two about where things will head. So giving people a canvas to try things and productizing the solutions they manually built is a good strategy. And so is, when you are doing product strategy, start with what solutions do you have today and what unique problems can you solve with them?
turns.zh: 我对团队说：写下你今天拥有的资产，然后写下你的信念，看看这两者之间在事物走向上是否有任何联系。所以，给人们一个尝试的框架，并把他们手动构建的解决方案产品化，是一个好策略。同样，在做产品战略时，从你今天拥有哪些解决方案以及你能用它们解决哪些独特问题开始。

turns.en: Got it. Okay. So it's nice to have here's the paths where starting with the solution's good. You're not saying always start with solution or it's always beneficial. And essentially in most cases you actually don't except in these two situations.
turns.zh: 明白了。好的。所以很高兴听到这些从解决方案出发的好路径。你并不是说总是从解决方案开始，或者它总是有益的。本质上在大多数情况下你其实并不这么做，除了这两种情况。

turns.en: Yes. I actually don't know if it's most cases, but it is important to understand the cases. I would say that a lot of customer discovery is by learning what customers are trying to do with your product and then trying to make that better. So you're actually observing a customer trying to create a solution for themselves in most products. And then you're like, oh, let me make that better for you. So it'll be fascinating to try to come up with a percentage. Is it most of the time you're actually implicitly starting with the manual customer solution, if you like? I think it's a good thing to think about as you go into do exploratory, which by the way with AI teams are doing enough of just talking to humans. It's become much easier to stay behind more dashboards.
turns.zh: 是的。我其实不知道是不是大多数情况，但理解这些情况很重要。我想说，很多客户发现是通过了解客户想用你的产品做什么，然后试着把它做得更好。所以在大多数产品中，你实际上是在观察客户试图为自己创造解决方案。然后你说，哦，让我帮你做得更好。所以试着想出一个百分比会很有趣。是不是大多数时候你其实是在隐含地从手动客户解决方案出发？我认为当你进行探索时，这是一个值得思考的好问题。顺便说一句，AI 团队现在做的人类对话已经够多了。躲在更多仪表盘后面变得容易多了。

turns.en: By the way, I didn't know you guys have this product, the whiteboard product. I didn't know that was a thing. So this is like Miro, FigJam-ish?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我不知道你们有这个产品，白板产品。我不知道还有这么个东西。所以这有点像 Miro、FigJam 那种？

turns.en: Yeah, Confluence whiteboards is huge. Yeah. So customers can embed whiteboards in Confluence and they add agents to them and they collaborate, real-time collaboration, and sticky notes turn them to Jira tickets, all that kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 是的，Confluence 白板非常庞大。是的。所以客户可以在 Confluence 中嵌入白板，并给它们添加智能体，他们可以协作，实时协作，便签可以变成 Jira 工单，诸如此类。

turns.en: So this is like a feature within Confluence. And it's okay, cool. All right. Folks don't know that it is, I didn't know it existed. This is great, good marketing for the whiteboard product.
turns.zh: 所以这就像是 Confluence 里的一个功能。好吧，酷。好了。大家不知道它存在，我之前也不知道。这很棒，对白板产品来说是很好的营销。

turns.en: Didn't intend it to be as marketing, but it's a good example I think. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没打算把它当营销，但我觉得这是个好例子。是的。

turns.en: Okay, cool. There's another counter narrative that you have, which is around AI and this kind of concern people have with just bolting AI onto stuff. And your feeling is that's actually good in many cases. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 好的，酷。你还有另一个反主流观点，是关于 AI 的，以及人们对直接把 AI 硬加上去的担忧。你觉得在很多情况下这其实是好事。谈谈这个吧。

turns.en: This is where the catchy headlines, Lenny. It is very catchy to say don't bolt AI into your product. You should reimagine the workflow. I certainly believe that. But however, the nuance is, I think if you have an established product, you have something ready today, the best way to reinvent your product to be AI native is to understand the flows that exist in your product and literally bolt on AI to them. Which sounds dirty. You may not market it that way, but actually, just think about it for a second. You've got a product. The product has millions of users. What I see some people doing and I talk to a few startups, they're like, or a few product companies, they're like, we're going to rewrite our product from scratch. I'm like, you don't think you can do that. But isn't the better way to actually work out how to evolve, not totally transform?
turns.zh: 这就是那些抓人眼球的标题，Lenny。说“不要直接把 AI 硬加到你的产品里，你应该重新构想工作流”非常抓人眼球。我当然相信这一点。但细微之处在于，我认为如果你有一个成熟的产品，你今天就有现成的东西，那么把你的产品重塑为 AI 原生的最佳方式，是理解你产品中已有的流程，然后直接把 AI 硬加上去。这听起来很脏。你可能不会那样营销，但实际上，你想一下。你有一个产品，这个产品有数百万用户。我看到一些人在做，我和一些初创公司聊过，他们就像，或者一些产品公司，他们说，我们要从头重写我们的产品。我说，你不觉得你能做到吧。但更好的方式难道不是弄清楚如何演进，而不是彻底转型吗？

turns.en: So the example I love to give is the Rover Agents one I just told you about, which is a good one. Customers have already modeled billions of business workflows in Jira. Just as an example, Jira is largely used by many non-software teams. It's a misconception most people have. For a while, you get an app approved in your App Store, it went through a ticketing system like Jira. It was Jira for a while, and then it goes through a whole review process. If you complain about your particular service with the telecom company, it goes through a Jira ticket. So customers have billions of workflows already modeled on our platform as an example. And so when it came to understanding how agents help humans move work forward, we looked at what are the human workflows that exist in the products. That's a good formula to go: what are the human workflows that exist in my product? Some of them are rigid workflows, as in someone's literally defined something. Some of them are informal workflows, like lowercase-w workflows. They're humans doing something. And then you can go, where can agents assist with steps of the workflow to generate new value, improve efficiency or something, whatever it is.
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢举的例子就是我刚跟你说的 Rover Agents，那是个好例子。客户已经在 Jira 中建模了数十亿的业务工作流。举个例子，Jira 被许多非软件团队广泛使用。这是大多数人的误解。有一段时间，你在应用商店上架一个应用，它要经过像 Jira 这样的工单系统。有一阵子就是 Jira，然后经过整个审核流程。如果你向电信公司投诉某项服务，它会经过一个 Jira 工单。所以客户已经在我们的平台上建模了数十亿的工作流，举个例子。所以当涉及到理解智能体如何帮助人类推进工作时，我们审视了产品中存在哪些人类工作流。这是一个好公式：我的产品中存在哪些人类工作流？有些是刚性工作流，就是有人字面上定义了什么。有些是非正式工作流，就像小写 w 的工作流。是人在做某事。然后你可以想，智能体可以在工作流的哪些步骤提供协助，以创造新价值、提高效率或其他什么。

turns.en: And so in Jira workflows, we basically added the ability to add agents to columns and cards and whatever. Is that bolting on? Let's use another term. Maybe if I was building an AI native work tracking tool, that's probably what I would do anyway. I would build the workflow and then let the agents work on bits of the workflow. And so my message to teams out there is like, hey, yes, reimagine the workflows. You should do that as an exercise. But look at where your customers are today. And if you have an established user base, an established user, it's your job to help them move from AI novice to AI native. And so you're trying to transition your customer cohort across as well. And so think about where they're working and where you can slowly introduce AI in those workflows.
turns.zh: 所以在 Jira 工作流中，我们基本上添加了将智能体添加到列和卡片等位置的能力。这算是硬加上去吗？我们换个说法。也许如果我在构建一个 AI 原生的工作跟踪工具，我可能也会这么做。我会构建工作流，然后让智能体在工作流的某些部分工作。所以我对团队传达的信息是：嘿，是的，重新构想工作流。你应该把这当作一个练习。但看看你的客户今天在哪里。如果你有一个成熟的用户群、成熟的用户，你的工作就是帮助他们从 AI 新手变成 AI 原生。所以你也在努力让你的客户群体完成过渡。所以想想他们在哪里工作，以及你可以在那些工作流的哪里慢慢引入 AI。

turns.en: So again, another misconception there. I think that from a marketing perspective, yeah, you probably wouldn't say bolt on, but literally we let you bolt on an agent to a Jira workflow and you stick it in a loop and then the agents work in loops and they run millions of times and they're measurable value. If it doesn't work, you kick the agent out or you make the emails better for the agent. There's a whole bunch of stuff you can do there.
turns.zh: 所以这又是一个误解。我认为从营销角度，你可能不会说“bolt on”，但字面上我们确实让你把一个智能体附加到 Jira 工作流上，你把它放进一个循环里，然后智能体就在循环中工作，运行数百万次，产生可衡量的价值。如果不行，你就把智能体踢出去，或者让给智能体的邮件更好。有很多事情可以做。

turns.en: I love all these takes. Before we started recording, I asked you what's the goal you have for this conversation and you talked about how we need more nuance in the conversation of building product. There's all these hot takes, these really viral clips that go out and people are like, oh, that's how I have to do it. And I'm guilty of people on this podcast saying a thing and then people at a company taking that and saying this is the way to do it. Lenny's podcast said that's the way to do it, which I hate. And so I love that that's kind of what you're trying to do here is add a lot more nuance to all these things people think are true. And show that it's not, you know, we've got all these spectrums and gradients that we've been talking about. Maybe just say more about that, why you think that's important.
turns.zh: 我喜欢所有这些观点。在我们开始录制之前，我问你这次对话的目标是什么，你谈到我们需要在构建产品的对话中增加更多细微差别。有所有这些热门观点，这些病毒式传播的片段，人们看了就说，哦，我就得这么做。我也有责任，这个播客上的人说了某件事，然后公司里的人就照搬，说这就是方法。Lenny 的播客说了这就是方法，我讨厌这样。所以我喜欢你想要做的就是给所有这些人们认为正确的事情增加更多细微差别。并表明事实并非如此，你知道，我们一直在谈论所有这些光谱和梯度。也许再多说一点，为什么你认为这很重要。

turns.en: You know, the classic thing in product I think especially is like every advice you've probably got on how to do product, someone probably has a counter totally opposite advice that works just as good. And again, you as a product team or a PM or a product leader, you're trying to understand the context in which their advice worked in. And that's where a lot of the nuance gets missed. You know, the builders one Lenny that we just talked about is a great example where I think zero to one projects, even in large organizations, you should put an AI builder type onto it. I'm fully convinced into that. But again, most organizations that have access to developers, this is not their problem. Their problem is where to direct the ship. So the context in which the advice is given is super important. Just like start with the solution, not the problem. I would equally advocate to start with the problem, but not enough people talk about the counter thing. It also just gives people confidence in like am I doing things the right way? And I'm like, is there a right way? If you do something and you've learned something, share it with the world. For a while I used to try to write blog posts about like I would share every craft lesson I've learned. One of the things we're talking about internally is that how do we scale product management inside Atlassian? And I go back to when I started at Atlassian, the window product managers on Confluence, the way we did that was these things called product engineers. And I learned what a product engineer was and I realized there was no term codified out there and I wrote a blog post about what I learned about product engineers. And you realize product engineers help product managers scale. They help you, they're the champions of that shared context that we talked about earlier, right? So all those nuances, I don't think it's talked about enough, but I appreciate you running these talks and hearing people out share their nuances. I think that's what needs to happen more.
turns.zh: 你知道，产品领域的经典情况是，你得到的关于如何做产品的每一条建议，可能都有人提出完全相反的建议，而且同样有效。作为产品团队、PM 或产品负责人，你要理解他们的建议在什么背景下有效。而很多细微差别就在那里被忽略了。我们刚才谈到的“构建者”就是一个很好的例子，我认为零到一的项目，即使在大公司里，也应该让 AI 构建者类型的人参与。我完全相信这一点。但再说一次，大多数有开发者的组织，这不是他们的问题。他们的问题是把船指向哪里。所以给出建议的上下文非常重要。就像“从解决方案开始，而不是问题”一样。我同样会主张从问题开始，但谈论相反观点的人不够多。这也能给人信心，比如我是不是在做正确的事？而我会想，有正确的方式吗？如果你做了某事并学到了东西，就与世界分享。有一段时间我尝试写博客，分享我学到的每一个技艺课程。我们内部正在讨论的一件事是，如何在 Atlassian 内部扩展产品管理？我回想起我刚加入 Atlassian 时，Confluence 的产品经理窗口，我们的方式是所谓的产品工程师。我了解了什么是产品工程师，我意识到外面没有这个术语的正式定义，于是我写了一篇关于我对产品工程师的了解的博客文章。你会发现产品工程师帮助产品经理扩展。他们帮助你，他们是我们在前面谈到的共享上下文的 champion，对吧？所以所有这些细微差别，我认为谈论得不够，但我感谢你主持这些对话，听取人们分享他们的细微差别。我认为这需要更多发生。

turns.en: Yeah, it's tough. I'm in a tough spot sometimes where people share an opinion and many people are like, that is wrong. Why did you give, why did you not push back on that? I find the best thing I can do that skills is have different perspectives here and not try to have everyone get everyone in line. This is the way to do it. And then people can decide here's what fits for me. Someone actually built a really fun project. I don't know if people know this. If you go to lennydata.com, you can actually connect an MCP that has all of my podcast transcripts. You're going to be in there. You're going to be slurped into this MCP soon. And it's also all my newsletter posts that you can use it any way you want. And somebody built, I think it was Nome actually, Nome Segal, built a tool that shows both sides of every debate.
turns.zh: 是的，这很难。我有时处于一个艰难的境地，人们分享一个观点，很多人就说，那是错的。你为什么给出，你为什么不反驳？我发现我能做的最好的事情就是在这里呈现不同的视角，而不是试图让所有人保持一致。这就是方法。然后人们可以决定什么适合我。有人实际上构建了一个非常有趣的项目。我不知道人们是否知道这个。如果你去 lennydata.com，你可以连接一个 MCP，里面有我所有的播客转录。你也会在那里。你很快就会被吸进这个 MCP。还有我所有的 newsletter 文章，你可以以任何方式使用。有人构建了，我想是 Nome，Nome Segal，构建了一个工具，展示每场辩论的双方观点。

turns.en: Oh, that's awesome. Like the contradictory advice?
turns.zh: 哦，那太棒了。就像矛盾的建议？

turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。

turns.en: That's so good. And then you want like that'll be a I'd love to see that dashboard and you'd love to see why it worked, like this advice and why it worked and this advice and why it worked. It's such a that's awesome. That's so good to see.
turns.zh: 那太好了。然后你会想要，我很想看到那个仪表盘，你会想看到为什么它有效，比如这个建议为什么有效，那个建议为什么有效。这真是，太棒了。很高兴看到。

turns.en: Is there anything you want to say that'll feed into this MCP that'll be forever part of the data set?
turns.zh: 你有什么想说的，会进入这个 MCP，永远成为数据集的一部分？

turns.en: I think I've given quite a few misconceptions here. So we've talked about misconceptions of builders, everyone's a builder. We've talked about the misconception of all PMs are the same. I think artist, scientist, general manager is one framework. You can do that. Misconception of PMs make all the decisions, right? I think that's another one we talked about. Oh, management. Management's another one, Lenny. So like everyone runs into their career in product management and usually in most organizations you hit a path where you... Hang on a second. I want to be involved in that strategy discussion, that strategy offsite. Oh, but it looks like the people that go to that thing or do that activity seem to be managers. I went through this experience myself. So therefore I need to manage. And they hit this fork in the career where they feel like that's the decision. And so the other I think misconception we need to help debunk is, you know, I think we try to do more of this at Atlassian. We have multiple distinguished product managers and engineers now where they work at the executive level. And so we're huge champions of the dual track career paths for individuals and managers. And a lot of people switch between both depending on the season they're in. Or they think they're starting a zero one. They'll go to managing a small team for a while and then they'll get big and they'll move back off. And we should celebrate that more because it plays to that person's strength. And so that's another misconception like to be involved in large strategic decisions at exec level at large companies. You need to be a manager. No, we have a lot of individual contributors that contribute at the exec level. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我想我在这里已经给出了不少误解。所以我们谈到了构建者的误解，每个人都是构建者。我们谈到了所有 PM 都一样的误解。我认为艺术家、科学家、总经理是一个框架。你可以这样做。PM 做所有决定的误解，对吧？我认为这是我们谈到的另一个。哦，管理。管理是另一个，Lenny。所以每个人在产品管理职业生涯中都会遇到，通常在大多数组织中你会遇到一条路径，你……等一下。我想参与那个战略讨论，那个战略务虚会。哦，但看起来去那个活动或做那个活动的人似乎是管理者。我自己经历过这个。所以因此我需要管理。他们遇到职业的分叉口，觉得那就是决定。所以我认为我们需要帮助揭穿的另一个误解是，你知道，我们在 Atlassian 试图做更多这样的事情。我们现在有多个杰出产品经理和工程师，他们在高管级别工作。所以我们是个体贡献者和管理者双轨职业路径的大力支持者。很多人根据他们所处的季节在两者之间切换。或者他们认为自己在启动零到一。他们会去管理一个小团队一段时间，然后团队变大，他们又退回来。我们应该更多地庆祝这一点，因为这发挥了那个人的优势。所以这是另一个误解，比如要在大型公司的高管级别参与重大战略决策。你需要是管理者。不，我们有很多个体贡献者在高管级别做出贡献。是的。

turns.en: Another sure counter narrative that I've been feeling which is that there's always talk of we don't need managers and that managers should be IC as well. And I feel like that's just not a good idea.
turns.zh: 另一个我一直感受到的反叙事是，总是有人说我们不需要管理者，管理者也应该是个体贡献者。我觉得那不是一个好主意。

turns.en: I feel like managers are actually very important. And to be a good manager, it's very hard to also do IC work—like meaningful IC work.
turns.zh: 我觉得管理者其实非常重要。而要成为一名优秀的管理者，同时还要做 IC（个人贡献者）的工作——有意义的 IC 工作——是非常困难的。

turns.en: It's really hard. So you can take two world views there if you're going to manage a lot. So take like 10, 15 people, or we want managers that will take three or four and own a project as well. And the reality is we have a mix of both at Atlassian. And again, try to play to each person's strength. And that's how you'll get the best outcome. And so do we have the span of control for managers? We generally try to say you should have at least three or four people minimum. I think most are in the eight or nine, something like that. But yeah, you do have some managers that will take on few people and will own projects. And some that will take on a lot and play a coach role a lot more.
turns.zh: 这真的很难。所以如果你要管理很多人，你可以采取两种世界观。比如带 10 到 15 个人，或者我们希望管理者带三到四个人，同时也负责一个项目。现实是，在 Atlassian，我们两者都有。而且，要尽量发挥每个人的优势。这样才能得到最好的结果。那么，我们有没有管理者的控制幅度？我们通常会说，你至少应该带三到四个人。我想大多数是八到九个人左右。但没错，你确实有一些管理者带的人少，同时负责项目。也有一些带很多人，更多地扮演教练角色。

turns.en: Let me ask you this: for new PM managers, so you just got into it, what do you find is the biggest issue that they run into, or thing they should probably be working on?
turns.zh: 让我问你这个问题：对于新晋的产品经理管理者，也就是刚进入管理岗位的人，你觉得他们遇到的最大问题是什么，或者他们应该着力改进的地方是什么？

turns.en: The number one thing I've seen is they go too hands-off too quickly. And they think that's the best behavior. It sounds a bit countercultural. I think the best leaders that we've ever had at Atlassian that continue to be there—the best managers, I shouldn't say managers, managers and leaders could be two separate things. You could have a leader who's a good manager, a manager who's not a good leader, and vice versa. So the best managers who are great leaders are able to go in with the team and help them get through outcomes. I can sit in a product review, Lenny, and be like, this isn't simple enough. And it's not like the team was sitting around going, all right, let's—oh, sorry, I forgot to write 'simple' to the agent. But the best managers are like, let's explore some options together, and they get in and they help the team work together and get through the outcome. I think that would be my number one observation: they get so hands-off and they're like, I'll just zoom out completely and let the team do that, which is good—you need to create space, don't get me wrong. But teams love it when they see managers lead by example. So I think it's going to be more important in all of AI.
turns.zh: 我见过的最主要问题是，他们太快地放手了。他们认为那是最好的行为。这听起来有点反文化。我认为我们在 Atlassian 有过的最好的领导者——那些继续留在那里的最好的管理者，我不该说管理者，管理者和领导者可能是两个不同的东西。你可能有一个领导者是好的管理者，一个管理者不是好的领导者，反之亦然。所以，最好的管理者同时也是伟大的领导者，他们能够和团队一起深入，帮助他们取得成果。Lenny，我可以坐在产品评审会上说，这不够简单。并不是团队坐在那里说，好吧，让我们——哦抱歉，我忘了给智能体写‘简单’了。但最好的管理者会说，让我们一起探索一些选项，然后他们深入进去，帮助团队协作并取得成果。我想那会是我的第一观察：他们变得太放手了，他们说，我就完全抽离，让团队去做，这很好——你需要创造空间，别误会我。但团队喜欢看到管理者以身作则。所以我认为在整个人工智能领域，这将更加重要。

turns.en: That's great advice. Okay, possibly final question. I've heard from a bunch of people that you work very closely with the founders and execs on the big product keynotes that the founders do.
turns.zh: 这是很好的建议。好的，可能是最后一个问题。我从很多人那里听说，你和创始人及高管密切合作，参与创始人做的大型产品主题演讲。

turns.en: I love keynotes.
turns.zh: 我喜欢主题演讲。

turns.en: Something most people don't say. You also work with the CEO and co-founders on their founder presentations, things like that. What's something you've learned about working with the top of the top that might be helpful for folks that are maybe struggling working with execs?
turns.zh: 这是大多数人不会说的话。你还和 CEO 及联合创始人合作他们的创始人演示等。关于与顶尖中的顶尖合作，你学到了什么可能对那些在与高管合作中挣扎的人有帮助的东西？

turns.en: There are so many—dangerous last question, Lenny. Without a doubt, I describe working with this as someone who's a strong visionary leader, often in founder-led companies—that's still the case, etc. It's like me and you watching a movie and they're on scene, you know, chapter 10 of the movie and you're on chapter three and the rest of the teams are on chapter one. And they're saying stuff and you're thinking, wait, what? Are you sure? That's everyone's first reaction. Now, you can do two things at that point as someone who works with that stakeholder or leader or vision leader. You can say, I'm going to follow orders and go do that and just pass that on. But the dangerous thing you do that is you're doing that with no conviction. You're doing that because the boss asked me to. Or your job could be—by the way, the vast majority of the time you could argue was a stakeholder or the founder right or wrong. My experience they've been right 99% of the time. It's just what I've realized is they've thought about that thing far more than anyone else. And the aha moments that got them there—my job now is to fill that context gap, to work out why did they get there and do I feel convicted of their thing? And I often start by like, I don't know man, I'm still working through this. What made you leave that conclusion? And I'm trying to get to chapter 10 as quickly as possible. And once I get to that, I know now what I need to do to bring the rest of the people along with me. So I would say often with these leaders they're thinking about things a lot. And trust—start by trusting. But it's not—I think the counter narrative here is the HIPPO—highest paid stakeholder, whatever, I can't remember the acronym—was the highest paid opinion
turns.zh: 有很多——危险的最后一个问题，Lenny。毫无疑问，我把与这种人的合作描述为与一位强大的有远见的领导者合作，通常是在创始人领导的公司里——情况仍然如此，等等。这就像我和你一起看电影，他们已经在电影的第 10 章，而你在第 3 章，其他团队在第 1 章。他们在说些什么，而你在想，等等，什么？你确定吗？这是每个人的第一反应。现在，作为与那个利益相关者或领导者或愿景领导者合作的人，你可以在那时做两件事。你可以说，我要服从命令去做那件事，然后把它传递下去。但你这样做的危险之处在于，你没有信念地去做。你这样做是因为老板要求我这样做。或者你的工作可能是——顺便说一句，大多数时候你可以争论利益相关者或创始人是对还是错。我的经验是，他们 99% 的时候是对的。我只是意识到，他们思考那件事比任何人都多。而让他们到达那里的顿悟时刻——我现在的工作是填补那个上下文差距，弄清楚他们为什么到达那里，以及我是否对他们的想法感到信服？我经常开始说，我不知道，伙计，我还在思考这个。是什么让你得出那个结论？我试图尽快到达第 10 章。一旦我到达那里，我现在知道我需要做什么来带领其他人一起前进。所以我会说，通常这些领导者思考事情很多。信任——从信任开始。但这不是——我认为这里的反叙事是 HIPPO——最高薪的利益相关者，随便，我记不住那个缩写——是最高薪的意见

turns.en: Person opinion
turns.zh: 个人意见

turns.en: Yeah, I can't spell people and I totally butchered that one.
turns.zh: 是的，我不会拼写‘people’，我完全搞砸了那个。

turns.en: Highest paid person
turns.zh: 最高薪的人

turns.en: Yeah, so I think the flip side is oh there's some stakeholder who thinks this is their pet project and whatever. I think that's certainly true in companies, don't get me wrong. But I think when you have someone that you know has thought about this domain particularly well, especially in the enterprise B2B space—you know I would say to someone like you can find if someone's worked in this space for several years, it is vastly different to I did a year here and I did a year there. It takes time to make large changes and whatever. And so assume they're right and assume you're wrong. And try to fill that context gap and sometimes you'll prove them wrong but it's not the goal here. The goal is to get the best outcome for customers. And so then you can bring the team along on the journey.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我认为另一面是，哦，有些利益相关者认为这是他们的宠物项目之类的。我认为在公司里这确实存在，别误会我。但我认为当你有一个你认识的人，他特别深入地思考过这个领域，尤其是在企业 B2B 领域——你知道我会对某人说，你可以发现如果一个人在这个领域工作了几年，这与我在这一年、那一年工作过是截然不同的。做出大的改变需要时间，等等。所以假设他们是对的，假设你是错的。并尝试填补那个上下文差距，有时你会证明他们错了，但这不是目标。目标是为客户取得最好的结果。然后你就可以带领团队一起踏上旅程。

turns.en: Let me ask you what happens if you actually disagree because I think a lot of people feel this like go through this and they're like that is a bad idea. Tips for handling that?
turns.zh: 让我问你，如果你实际上不同意怎么办，因为我认为很多人感觉像经历这个，他们会说那是个坏主意。处理这个的技巧是什么？

turns.en: So if you feel like you've caught up to the aha moment and you're still disagreeing and you feel like you have a good case for why you disagree, I will still state that. And then I will state, is this something you have crazy conviction for? And I'll say, are you the decision maker or am I? Like I'll ask that. Common question is who owns this decision? Like just be super transparent. And if they really feel like I would like to take this decision or I want you to decide—I disagree, but I want you to decide, but which by the way they do a lot more than you'd imagine—like they'd be like I disagree with this, but I want you to own that decision. But I will back you if I disagree and I will back you and move along with it. So transparency is key to foster that relationship.
turns.zh: 所以如果你觉得你已经赶上了那个顿悟时刻，你仍然不同意，并且你觉得你有很好的理由说明为什么你不同意，我仍然会陈述这一点。然后我会说，这是你有疯狂信念的事情吗？我会说，你是决策者还是我是？我会问这个。常见的问题是谁拥有这个决策？就像超级透明。如果他们真的觉得我想做这个决定，或者我想让你决定——我不同意，但我想让你决定，但顺便说一句，他们这样做的次数比你想象的多得多——他们会说，我不同意这个，但我想让你拥有那个决定。但如果你不同意，我会支持你，我会支持你并继续推进。所以透明度是培养这种关系的关键。

turns.en: So but what do you do when you're communicating it to your team and you disagree anything there? Is it stand behind it always?
turns.zh: 那么，但是当你向团队传达并且你不同意时，你该怎么做？总是支持它吗？

turns.en: Oh no, I'll present both arguments.
turns.zh: 哦不，我会提出双方论点。

turns.en: I will state why I believe one argument is more superior than another and I'll equally argue for the opposite. There was a recent example where we were branding a particular thing and I think it was like the best of the worst options we can make. And I'll say I think here are the pros, here are the cons and if you argue for the opposite, I think here are the pros, here are the cons. We have decided to make this decision. I'll try not to call the individual out. And they're both legitimate trade-offs. And we're moving ahead with this one. And you need to speak the room of what the other opposite argument that everyone's thinking and represent that appropriately. The best PMs I find can argue against themselves and present you really good reasons why they shouldn't do the thing. The really blind ones will be like, oh yeah, my thing's the best. We should definitely do this option. It's the best option of all. Then I often say, why would we not do this? I love asking that in reviews. And then sometimes like I haven't thought about why we wouldn't do this. And I'm like, you should argue for the opposite as well and feel like you've intellectually wrestled with that and then move forward.
turns.zh: 我会说明为什么我认为一个论点比另一个更优越，并且同样为相反的观点辩护。最近有一个例子，我们在为某个东西做品牌命名，我认为那是我能做出的最不坏的选择。我会说，我认为优点是这些，缺点是这些；如果你为相反的观点辩护，我认为优点是这些，缺点是这些。我们已经决定做出这个决定。我会尽量避免点名个人。两者都是合理的权衡。我们正在推进这个方案。你需要说出房间里其他人正在想的相反论点，并恰当地代表它。我发现最好的产品经理能够反驳自己，并给你很好的理由说明为什么他们不应该做这件事。而那些非常盲目的产品经理会说，哦对，我的东西是最好的。我们肯定应该做这个选项。这是所有选项中最好的。然后我经常问，为什么我们不这样做？我喜欢在评审中问这个。有时他们会说，我没想过为什么我们不做这个。我就说，你也应该为相反的观点辩护，感觉你在智力上与之搏斗过，然后继续前进。

turns.en: That is great advice. Something that I'll mention briefly: when someone with power shares an opinion, a lot of times people take it as that is what we need to do. And Dharmesh Shah has this really great framework he calls flash tags. I don't know if you know this,
turns.zh: 这是很好的建议。我简要提一点：当有权力的人分享一个观点时，很多时候人们会把它当作我们必须做的事情。Dharmesh Shah 有一个很棒的框架，他称之为闪存标签。我不知道你是否知道这个，

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 知道。

turns.en: where he basically says okay, he's like hashtag FYI. So when he shares an opinion, it's like okay, this is just an FYI or this is a suggestion or this is a recommendation or this is a plea. And it's a nice way for someone that implicitly has power to communicate okay, this is how I feel. Just an FYI, you don't have to do this or it's a plea, please do it.
turns.zh: 他基本上说，比如标签为 #FYI。所以当他分享一个观点时，就像是说，这只是供参考，或者这是一个建议，或者这是一个推荐，或者这是一个请求。这是一种很好的方式，让那些隐含拥有权力的人传达：好的，这就是我的感受。只是供参考，你不必这样做；或者这是一个请求，请这样做。

turns.en: Yeah, and I'll say those are like our founders do that as well quite a bit. They'll say strong opinion, not my decision, blah blah blah. I will tell but often you'll get people just in a discussion, they won't pre-hashtag their discussion as they talk. And so I'll say to PMs, your job as a PM is to be the person in the room to ask that clarifying question on level of conviction on the topic. And you know, just to be clear, you know, the classic playback technique at the very end, but like as part of that process be like this is a conviction we will go and explore further or this is something we will take as input and then make the decision ourselves and be clear with that. So I'll put that back on the PM sometimes cuz the stakeholder doesn't always do the hashtag at the end of or before or whatever it is, you know what I mean?
turns.zh: 是的，我会说我们的创始人也会经常这样做。他们会说“强烈观点，不是我的决定”等等。但通常你会遇到人们在讨论中，他们不会在说话时预先加上标签。所以我会对产品经理说，你作为产品经理的工作就是在房间里问那个澄清问题，关于对这个话题的信念程度。你知道，为了明确，你知道，经典的复述技巧在最后，但作为这个过程的一部分，要说这是我们将进一步探索的信念，或者这是我们将作为输入然后自己做出决定的事情，并明确这一点。所以有时我会把这一点推回给产品经理，因为利益相关者并不总是在最后或之前加上标签，你明白我的意思吗？

turns.en: I know, man. Feel like we could talk for hours of all the tips and tricks and tactics you've learned this could go on forever. I'm going to end it here so that we have time for another episode someday to go deeper. But before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you wanted to share, anything else you want to double down on before we get to our lightning round?
turns.zh: 我知道，伙计。感觉我们可以聊上几个小时，关于你学到的所有技巧和战术，这可以永远继续下去。我要在这里结束，以便我们有一天有时间再深入探讨另一集。但在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电轮之前，你还有什么想分享的吗，还有什么想强调的，在我们进入闪电轮之前？

turns.en: I think to your listeners, nuance, I think we've talked about the nuance is important, so please share your stories. I think the other thing I would just highlight is you're a product of someone else creating opportunities for you. So ask yourself who are you creating opportunities for? And if you can't think of that name listening to this podcast or watching it, try to find someone that you can champion, be a voice for etc. because you believe in them and you want to give them a go and that kind of stuff. So, just remember where you came from is a long way of saying that.
turns.zh: 我想对你的听众说，细微差别，我想我们谈过细微差别很重要，所以请分享你的故事。我想强调的另一件事是，你是别人为你创造机会的产物。所以问问自己，你在为谁创造机会？如果你在听这个播客或看它时想不出那个名字，试着找到一个你可以支持的人，为他们发声等等，因为你相信他们，你想给他们一个机会等等。所以，记住你来自哪里，这是表达这一点的一种冗长方式。

turns.en: I love that. Well, Sharif, with that we have reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。好的，Sharif，至此我们已经到了非常激动人心的闪电轮。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.en: Let's go.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.en: Let's go. First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。第一个问题，你发现自己最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.en: Look, I read with my kids a lot or read books with my kids. Lately we're reading the Prison Healer by Yvette Noni, I think her name is. It's a like a fantasy book in a prison scene, dystopian prison kind of escape story. Awesome read with my kids. I personally read the Bible a lot. I think it's a book that I just keep coming back and meditating to and gives me some kind of grounding in the world of where AI is headed as well. But like most of my books are kids books. The other one I read with my kids, Wing Feather Saga is such a good read. It's about a bunch of kids who are heirs to a kingdom and they don't know that they overcome adversity to get there and stuff in it. So, I read a lot of kids books. Yeah.
turns.zh: 看，我经常和孩子们一起读书。最近我们在读 Yvette Noni 的《监狱疗愈者》，我想她的名字是。这是一本奇幻书，背景是监狱场景，反乌托邦监狱的逃脱故事。和孩子们一起读很棒。我个人经常读《圣经》。我认为这是一本我不断回来冥想并给我一些关于 AI 走向的根基的书。但我的大部分书都是儿童书。我和孩子们读的另一本是《翼羽传奇》，非常好看。它是关于一群孩子，他们是王国的继承人，他们不知道他们克服逆境到达那里等等。所以，我读了很多儿童书。是的。

turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目？

turns.en: Project Hail Mary was awesome. I mean I cried a lot of movies, so it's probably a better like yeah, just totally loved it. Awesome watch, very thought provoking, emotional.
turns.zh: 《万福玛丽计划》很棒。我的意思是我看很多电影都哭了，所以这可能是更好的，是的，完全喜欢它。很棒的观看体验，非常发人深省，情感丰富。

turns.en: Fun fact, my cousin is the Russian scientist in that movie.
turns.zh: 有趣的事实，我的表亲是那部电影里的俄罗斯科学家。

turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.en: A little somewhat distant cousin, but still related. She's killing it. Okay, next question, favorite slash most interesting AI products that you've recently discovered or just are really hooked on?
turns.zh: 有点远房的表亲，但仍然有亲戚关系。她做得很好。好的，下一个问题，你最近发现或真正迷上的最喜欢/最有趣的 AI 产品？

turns.en: This is total recency bias. I mean there's a few favorite AI products, but like I'm just going to go with a massive recency bias. We were on a long drive with the kids and Google Maps added Gemini to Google Maps, at least in Australia and Apple CarPlay. I don't know if you've seen that or not. And so when we drive, we typically put on sometimes we put on music, sometimes we put on AI and play a game. We play like a road trip game or we'll play a quiz game and we'll take turns or whatever it is. We everyone will be yelling at the AI while we're driving. It's very entertaining. But it's was fascinating to see in the map view Gemini added because we just pressed the like it's such a lesson in product workflow proximity. Like I'm in the map. I'm not going to close it off and switch and open one of the AIs to talk to it. I'm just going to chat to Gemini right here. But it's super contextual to the trip. So be like, hey, we're heading to this destination and we started playing some fun quiz games about the destination we're going to etc. And it was just one of those delightful experiences in the car that I'm like that was awesome. It was a fun experience. I could still see the map and talk to the AI at the same time. The kids had a blast. So it was entertaining. Got them off the screens for at least 30 minutes.
turns.zh: 这完全是近因偏差。我的意思是，有一些最喜欢的 AI 产品，但我只是要选择巨大的近因偏差。我们和孩子们进行了一次长途驾驶，Google Maps 在澳大利亚和 Apple CarPlay 中至少添加了 Gemini 到 Google Maps。我不知道你是否见过。所以当我们开车时，我们通常会放音乐，有时我们会打开 AI 玩游戏。我们玩公路旅行游戏或问答游戏，轮流玩等等。每个人都会在开车时对 AI 大喊大叫。非常有趣。但在地图视图中看到 Gemini 添加进来真是令人着迷，因为我们只是按了，这真是产品工作流邻近性的一个教训。就像我在地图里。我不会关闭它并切换打开一个 AI 来与它交谈。我就在这里和 Gemini 聊天。但它与旅行超级相关。所以就像，嘿，我们要去这个目的地，我们开始玩一些关于我们要去的目的地的有趣问答游戏等等。这只是车里那些令人愉快的体验之一，我就像那太棒了。这是一次有趣的体验。我仍然可以看到地图并同时与 AI 交谈。孩子们玩得很开心。所以很有趣。至少让他们离开了屏幕 30 分钟。

turns.en: Did they just bolt AI onto it?
turns.zh: 他们只是把 AI 螺栓固定在上面吗？

turns.en: Oh, nice. I like how you did that.
turns.zh: 哦，不错。我喜欢你这样做。

turns.en: Call back.
turns.zh: 回调。

turns.en: Two final questions. Favorite life motto. Is there a motto you often come back to in work or in life that you find really useful?
turns.zh: 最后两个问题。最喜欢的座右铭。有没有一句你在工作或生活中经常回味、觉得非常有用的座右铭？

turns.en: People tell me I'm very relaxed and fun at work and always joking. It's usually how I deal with my nerves to be honest, Lenny. But they ask me like why etc. And I'm always reminded that you as a person should decouple yourself from your job identity, which is really hard especially in the world of tech. And celebrate the individual outside their work life, I think is an important thing that we don't do enough. And you know, I love playing footy which is like flag tag with a bunch of folks who live locally and none of them work in tech. And they're just a mix of electricians and bricklayers and whatever and different jobs. But they're amazing human beings that don't work in technology. And so reminding people to decouple themselves from their job as their identity I think is something that's healthy and will keep you sustainable in your work and in your personal life as well.
turns.zh: 人们说我在工作中非常放松、有趣，总是开玩笑。说实话，Lenny，这通常是我应对紧张的方式。但他们问我为什么等等。我总是提醒自己，作为一个人，你应该把自我与工作身份脱钩，这在科技界尤其难。庆祝工作之外的个体，我认为是一件重要的事，我们做得不够。你知道，我喜欢玩足球，就像腰旗橄榄球，和一群住在当地的人一起玩，他们都不在科技行业工作。他们是电工、砖瓦匠等等不同职业的混合。但他们是了不起的人，不在科技行业工作。所以提醒人们把自我与工作身份脱钩，我认为是健康的，会让你在工作和个人生活中都保持可持续。

turns.en: I will share a quote that has come up a couple times on this podcast that always hits people right in the heart. The only people that will remember that you worked late are your kids.
turns.zh: 我想分享一句在这个播客上出现过几次的话，它总是直击人心。唯一会记得你加班到很晚的人是你的孩子。

turns.en: So true. I've read a similar one which is nobody goes to a funeral and the tombstone like it's saying on tombstone this person worked so hard or whatever like that's never in the eulogy or whatever so that's another motivator yeah.
turns.zh: 太对了。我读过类似的一句：没有人去葬礼时，墓碑上会写着这个人工作非常努力之类的，悼词里永远不会出现这些，所以这是另一个动力。

turns.en: All right final question I've been wondering what is going on behind you? There's like all these fun things that happening what is this explain?
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个问题，我一直想知道你背后是什么？好像有很多有趣的东西，这是什么，解释一下？

turns.en: Atlassian t-shirt culture we make a t-shirt often to tell a story about a moment in our history. So this is like confluence questions was an app that was when we had our first QA team that was when we launched a Vietnam office. There's a story behind each one of these shirts and I love collecting them just a great way to tell stories when the bigger you get the stories become more important to tell the teams and I've got hundreds of these shirts and one day my wife ripped up my shirts and surprised me for a thing she did for my birthday and created up this giant plaque this huge shirt and stitched together some of my favorite shirts that have stories behind each one of them so that's what that is.
turns.zh: Atlassian 的 T 恤文化，我们经常制作 T 恤来讲述公司历史中某个时刻的故事。比如这件是 Confluence Questions，那是一个应用，当时我们有了第一个 QA 团队，也是我们开设越南办公室的时候。每件 T 恤背后都有一个故事，我喜欢收集它们，这是一种很好的讲故事方式，公司越大，故事对团队来说就越重要。我有几百件这样的 T 恤，有一天我妻子把我的 T 恤剪了，为我生日准备了一个惊喜，制作了这个巨大的牌匾，这件巨大的 T 恤，把我最喜欢的一些有故事的 T 恤缝在一起，所以就是这个。

turns.en: That's very sweet. I could see that going horribly wrong. What did you do to my shirts? I've been saving these for years.
turns.zh: 太贴心了。我能想象这可能会搞砸。你对我的 T 恤做了什么？我保存这些好多年了。

turns.en: I wrote a blog internally that was titled my wife ripped up my Atlassian shirts and people like what and then they read the details and whatever but then for our recent 20-year anniversary as a company I just walked through 110 shirts and recorded a video on YouTube it was a lot of fun and just like the story behind each one it was just very satisfying.
turns.zh: 我在内部写了一篇博客，标题是“我妻子撕了我的 Atlassian T 恤”，人们一开始很惊讶，然后读了细节等等。但后来在我们公司最近的 20 周年纪念时，我回顾了 110 件 T 恤，并在 YouTube 上录制了一个视频，非常有趣，就像每件 T 恤背后的故事，非常令人满足。

turns.en: Let me ask you this what's unique cultural ritual of Atlassian that might be fun for people to learn of?
turns.zh: 让我问问你，Atlassian 有什么独特的文化仪式，可能让人们觉得有趣并想了解？

turns.en: There's a lot. We are an incredibly transparent company. Open company is one of our values. Like as in every exec review is usually recorded, available to search and find and loom and ask questions and you know run the AI agent through it. So the transparency here, everyone that joins says I've never experienced anything like it. I mean I haven't started a lesson for a long time so I'm used to it, but they're like oh my gosh, when do you stop reading? Like there's so much content. So I would say open by default is the ironically Lenny. I think it's also I mean partly because of confluence and the nature of we have of the product we have. People just document and create and it's open by default. But sharing context is key in the world of AI and so having an open by default approach to things is actually better in the long run for you as a company because they're by definition it means there's more context that the AI has access to and the humans have access to. So the openness is unbelievable here, but it's pretty crazy, but people love it.
turns.zh: 有很多。我们是一家极其透明的公司。开放公司是我们的价值观之一。比如每次高管会议通常都会被录制，可以搜索、查找、用 Loom 录制并提问，你知道，还可以让 AI 智能体处理。所以这里的透明度，每个加入的人都说我从未经历过这样的。我的意思是，我很久没有开始新的一课了，所以我习惯了，但他们说天哪，你什么时候停止阅读？内容太多了。所以我会说“默认开放”是讽刺的，Lenny。我认为这也部分是因为 Confluence 和我们产品的性质。人们只是记录和创造，默认就是开放的。但在 AI 世界里，共享上下文是关键，所以对事情采取默认开放的方法，从长远来看对公司实际上更好，因为顾名思义，这意味着 AI 和人类可以访问更多的上下文。所以这里的开放程度令人难以置信，但相当疯狂，不过人们喜欢它。

turns.en: That is super interesting. There's been a number of companies over time that have done this. GitLab is a good example. And it's interesting now with AI being able to read all of the things and tell you what you need to know. It changes that and like in theory you could like it might expose things that maybe people shouldn't have seen much more easily and quickly. On the other hand, it gives you all the context as you described to make better decisions.
turns.zh: 这非常有趣。随着时间的推移，有很多公司这样做过。GitLab 就是一个很好的例子。有趣的是，现在 AI 能够阅读所有内容并告诉你需要知道什么。这改变了情况，理论上它可能更容易、更快速地暴露一些人们可能不应该看到的东西。另一方面，正如你描述的，它为你提供了所有上下文，以便做出更好的决策。

turns.en: I have this theory Lenny. So we have a team anywhere policy so you can work any way you like. We have a legal entity so some people choose to work remote a lot. Some people don't. And so just as an example, you know when I have part of my team is in the West Coast of the USA. They a lot of them like an in office culture. And for reasons and some people in the APAC region love a distributed culture. I have a theory we're trying to prove out right now, hypothesis, which is those that are remote are more likely to get more outcomes out of AI then those are co-located.
turns.zh: 我有一个理论，Lenny。我们有“团队无处不在”的政策，所以你可以以任何方式工作。我们有法律实体，所以有些人选择经常远程工作，有些人不。举个例子，你知道，我团队的一部分在美国西海岸。他们很多人喜欢办公室文化。而亚太地区的一些人喜欢分布式文化。我有一个理论，我们正在试图证明，假设是：远程的人比同地办公的人更有可能从 AI 中获得更多成果。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And so we're just got a bunch of data scientists trying to prove that out right now, so that'll be a fascinating theory. And the thing here is that you just tend to write more and share more digitally when you're remote.
turns.zh: 所以我们有一群数据科学家正在试图证明这一点，这将是一个迷人的理论。这里的问题是，当你远程工作时，你倾向于写更多、更多地进行数字分享。

turns.en: And consume. Yeah.
turns.zh: 还有消费。是的。

turns.en: Yeah, and when you're in person you just whiteboard more or whatever and they're both good approaches and you need both. But it's again maybe another counterpoint of the going back to in-office culture maybe.
turns.zh: 是的，当你面对面时，你只是更多地使用白板之类的，两者都是好方法，你都需要。但这也许又是回到办公室文化的另一个反例。

turns.en: Going back to this report that I'm putting out actually remote work has plateaued. There's no it's kind of stalled at 10 15 20% across industries, so that'll be interesting to watch if that grows again with AI. Anyway, I keep asking you questions, but we should wrap up. Sharif, this was awesome. This was such a great deep important conversation that I think is going to help a lot of people. You're talking about opportunity. I think this is going to open up a lot of new opportunities for folks, so thank you so much for being here. Any is there some way that listeners can be useful to you? That's my final question that I almost forgot to ask.
turns.zh: 回到我即将发布的这份报告，实际上远程工作已经趋于平稳。没有，它在各行业停滞在 10%、15%、20%，所以如果随着 AI 再次增长，那将很有趣。不管怎样，我一直在问你问题，但我们应该结束了。Sharif，这太棒了。这是一次非常深入、重要的对话，我认为会帮助很多人。你在谈论机会。我认为这将为人们开辟许多新机会，所以非常感谢你来到这里。有没有什么方式可以让听众对你有用？这是我差点忘记问的最后一个问题。

turns.en: If you see something in social media — a lovely tag headline on one line, "you shouldn't hire juniors anymore," or whatever it is you see — be the person that asks the nuanced questions. Be like, "What? Why did that work for you? Why didn't that work for you?" Don't be the person that amplifies that one view without first understanding the context. I think that applies to many things in society, not just product, but yeah.
turns.zh: 如果你在社交媒体上看到点什么——一行抓眼球的标题，“你不该再招初级员工了”，或者你看到的任何东西——请做那个提出细致问题的人。就像：“什么？为什么那对你有用？为什么那对你没用？”不要做那个还没先理解背景就放大单一观点的人。我觉得这适用于社会上的很多事情，不只是产品，但就是这样。

turns.en: Nuance.
turns.zh: 细致。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Amazing. Sharif, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Sherif，非常感谢你来做客。

turns.en: Appreciate the time and the opportunity. Thanks, Lenny.
turns.zh: 感谢你给的时间和机会。谢谢，Lenny。

turns.en: I appreciate you. Bye, everyone. Thank you so much for listening. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 感谢你。大家再见。非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期有价值，可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或你常用的播客应用上订阅节目。另外，也请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，这能真正帮助其他听众发现这个播客。你可以在 lennyspodcast.com 找到所有往期节目，或了解更多关于节目的信息。下期见。

consensus.en: PMs own decision-making velocity, not decisions; their core job is filling context gaps.
consensus.zh: 产品经理负责决策速度，而非决策本身；核心工作是填补上下文缺口。

consensus.en: Build a shared brain across customer, product/market, and business context to scale teams.
consensus.zh: 围绕客户、产品/市场、业务三类上下文构建共享大脑，以实现团队规模化。

consensus.en: AI amplifies strengths and weaknesses; domain expertise and taste still matter most.
consensus.zh: AI 会放大优势与劣势；领域专长和品味仍然最重要。

consensus.en: Diverse teams and complementary skills are more important than ever in the AI era.
consensus.zh: 在 AI 时代，多元化团队和互补技能比以往更重要。

consensus.en: Hire juniors for new ways of working; seniors identify AI slop and ensure quality.
consensus.zh: 招聘初级员工带来新工作方式；资深员工识别 AI 垃圾并确保质量。

consensus.en: Start with existing workflows and bolt on AI to evolve products, not rewrite from scratch.
consensus.zh: 从现有工作流出发，通过附加 AI 来演进产品，而非从头重写。

contrarian.en: PMs should not ship code; direction, not throughput, is the bottleneck in scaled orgs.
contrarian.zh: 产品经理不应写代码；在规模化组织中，方向而非吞吐量才是瓶颈。

contrarian.en: PMs are often poor solution designers; access to tools doesn't equal domain expertise.
contrarian.zh: 产品经理往往是糟糕的解决方案设计师；能使用工具不等于具备领域专长。

contrarian.en: Starting with a solution can be valid for discovery and strategy, not always the problem.
contrarian.zh: 从解决方案出发在发现和战略中可能有效，并非总是从问题开始。

contrarian.en: Bolting AI onto existing products is often the best way to become AI-native.
contrarian.zh: 将 AI 附加到现有产品上通常是实现 AI 原生的最佳方式。

contrarian.en: You still need to hire juniors; they bring AI-native ways of working that seniors lack.
contrarian.zh: 仍然需要招聘初级员工；他们带来资深员工缺乏的 AI 原生工作方式。

contrarian.en: Managers should stay hands-on and lead by example, not go hands-off too quickly.
contrarian.zh: 管理者应保持亲力亲为、以身作则，而非过早放手。
